regions.text: to CUDA as someone with 10 years of performance engineering and distributed sys tems experience. I came to it as a curious person who wanted to understand what was happening underneath the deep learning tools I was already using. When I first tried to learn CUDA for deep learning, I often found myself missing the connective tissue between ideas. I could find explanations of CUDA mechanics, and I could find examples of sophisticated kernels, but I still had to work out how the pieces lined up: how threads map to tensors, how memory access patterns become perfor mance problems, how reductions show up inside ordinary model operations, and why attention changes the shape of the whole optimization problem.

regions.label: abstract
regions.text: I wrote this book because it is the one I wanted when I was starting out. I did not come to CUDA as someone with 10 years of performance engineering and distributed sys tems experience. I came to it as a curious person who wanted to understand what was happening underneath the deep learning tools I was already using. When I first tried to learn CUDA for deep learning, I often found myself missing the connective tissue between ideas. I could find explanations of CUDA mechanics, and I could find examples of sophisticated kernels, but I still had to work out how the pieces lined up: how threads map to tensors, how memory access patterns become perfor mance problems, how reductions show up inside ordinary model operations, and why attention changes the shape of the whole optimization problem. That process of connecting the dots became this book. Many of these concepts were not perfectly clear to me the first time I encountered them. Writing the chapters forced me to slow down, build the examples, test the kernels, check the performance claims, and teach each idea back carefully enough that I knew I understood it. The result is a path through CUDA that follows the order in which the pieces became clear to me. I think that perspective matters. An expert who has lived in this world for a decade can forget which steps are nonobvious at the beginning. I tried to keep those steps visible: what the GPU is doing, why the code is shaped the way it is, where the profiler is pointing, and how a small kernel-level choice connects to the larger deep learning workload. Just as important is knowing when not to write custom CUDA. Most of the time, a high-quality framework operation, vendor library, or generated kernel is the right answer. The book starts with the foundations: kernels, threads, blocks, memory transfers, indexing, and simple neural network operations. From there it moves into increasingly realistic deep learning kernels: transformer inference, GEMV and GEMM, softmax, layer normalization, top-k, tensor cores, Flash Attention, quantization, distributed com munication, and CUTLASS. Each topic is tied back to the same question: what is the GPU doing, and how should that change the code we write? Throughout the book, you will profile kernels, reason about memory bandwidth and occupancy, compare implementation strategies, and learn when a custom CUDA ker nel is worth its complexity. The point is not to replace frameworks for the sake of it. The point is to understand the layer beneath PyTorch, JAX, TensorRT, and other high-level tools well enough to make better performance decisions.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Who should read this book This book is for engineers, researchers, and technically curious builders who use deep learning systems and want to understand what happens below the framework layer: AI and machine learning engineers who want lower latency or cheaper inference than the default framework path provides, systems and performance engineers moving into GPU work, and researchers who need to verify, debug, or extend the kernels their models depend on.

regions.text: The appendices collect the practical reference material: appendix A covers installation and setup; appendix B documents how to run each chapter’s code examples; appendix C is a troubleshooting and development-practice guide; appendix D gathers command references, CUDA templates, and Python kernel bindings; and appendix E lists addi tional resources for continued learning. The repository is organized by chapter, and appendix B walks through building and running every example, including the exact compiler flags and the hardware each example was verified on. Chapters 7 through 11 each stand on that foundation and can be read selectively, though they are ordered so that each one deepens the performance story of the one before it.

regions.text: About the code This book contains many examples of source code, both in numbered listings and in line with normal text. In both cases, source code is formatted in a fixed-width font like this to separate it from ordinary text. Annotations accompany many of the list ings, highlighting important concepts. You can get executable snippets of code from the liveBook (online) version of this book at https: / /livebook.manning.com/book/cuda-for- llms . The complete code for the examples in the book is available for download from the book’s GitHub repository at https: / /github.com/infatoshi/book.cu and from the Manning website at https: / / www.manning.com/books/cuda-for- llms . The repository is organized by chapter, and appendix B walks through building and running every example, including the exact compiler flags and the hardware each example was verified on. The kernels were val idated on consumer hardware (an RTX 3090), with the tensor core and distributed material additionally verified on data center GPUs (H100). You do not need data cen ter hardware to follow the book: appendix A includes cloud options, and every chap ter’s core examples run on a single consumer GPU.

regions.text: about the author

regions.label: text
regions.text: Elliot Arledge created the official 12-hour CUDA course for FreeCodeCamp. He also authored a course on large language model creation for FreeCodeCamp. He is a trainer and independent consultant on CUDA and deep learning performance optimization. He has developed a visual teaching style using common objects like rectangles, cubes, and prisms to introduce and demonstrate complex topics like softmax, tensors, embeddings, and attention.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Large language models (LLMs) consume staggering compute budgets. The differ ence between a model that trains in days rather than weeks, or infers in milliseconds rather than seconds, often comes down to how effectively you use GPU hardware. That optimization happens in CUDA, the layer PyTorch calls into when it runs on an NVIDIA GPU.

regions.text: When do you need custom CUDA? 3

regions.label: footer
regions.text: only supports new patterns like sliding window attention but is also optimized for the lat est hardware, such as B200 tensor cores. The kernel must also plug into the framework’s automatic differentiation system (the machinery that computes gradients during train ing, so users can call loss.backward() without thinking about the underlying math). This kind of work builds the foundational tools other developers rely on. Similarly, a kernel engineer at a company like xAI working on a large language model might profile their training pipeline and discover that standard attention kernels don’t scale to their massive context lengths. Their job is to write custom kernels that can efficiently handle sequences of over a million tokens (the individual units a language model reads, roughly corresponding to words or subwords). This involves developing clever tiling strategies to minimize memory usage and tuning the kernel to achieve max imum throughput on their specific cluster hardware. A custom CUDA implementation in this context could deliver a 2–3× speedup, which translates directly into millions of dollars in savings on training and inference costs. The edge deployment engineer at a robotics company faces a different set of constraints. They need to deploy vision models on power-constrained embedded GPUs, which require real-time inference with latencies under 10 milliseconds. Standard framework operations are often too slow or power hungry. This engineer writes custom CUDA programs to fuse multiple operations, reducing memory bandwidth, a common bottle neck. They might also implement custom int8 quantization and dequantization kernels and tune their code for the unique memory layout of edge-class GPUs to enable appli cations like autonomous drones and self-driving cars. An algorithms researcher developing a novel architecture might need custom CUDA to demonstrate competitive performance. Although many new operations can be com posed from existing PyTorch primitives, some genuinely require custom implemen tations. The FlashAttention paper ( https: / /arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135 ), for example, required custom CUDA to achieve its memory efficiency gains.

regions.label: footer
regions.text: But can you actually beat PyTorch and Hugging Face? Yes, often you can, and you do not need decades of GPU experience to start. Sev eral of the kernel-optimization walk-throughs in later chapters were inspired by, and in places refactored from, work done by people who were themselves early in their ker nel-engineering journey. They were not career CUDA programmers; they were curious engineers who picked up the right reference material, followed a careful step-by-step optimization path, and were able to beat the corresponding PyTorch baselines on spe cific GPUs with surprisingly few hours of hand optimization.

regions.label: footer
regions.text: Once you accept that humans without a heroic background can do this, the next step is mechanical: give an LLM the same step-by-step documentation, the same refer ence material, and the same direction, and it can do the same thing autonomously. That is what the companion benchmark suite at https://kernelbench.com does. It runs a combinatorial sweep across GPU architectures, frontier models, and kernel problems, asking LLMs to write CUDA and Triton kernels and then grading the results

Similarly, a kernel engineer at a company like xAI working on a large language model might profile their training pipeline and discover that standard attention kernels don’t scale to their massive context lengths. Their job is to write custom kernels that can efficiently handle sequences of over a million tokens (the individual units a language model reads, roughly corresponding to words or subwords). This involves developing clever tiling strategies to minimize memory usage and tuning the kernel to achieve max imum throughput on their specific cluster hardware. A custom CUDA implementation in this context could deliver a 2–3× speedup, which translates directly into millions of dollars in savings on training and inference costs. The edge deployment engineer at a robotics company faces a different set of constraints. They need to deploy vision models on power-constrained embedded GPUs, which require real-time inference with latencies under 10 milliseconds. Standard framework operations are often too slow or power hungry. This engineer writes custom CUDA programs to fuse multiple operations, reducing memory bandwidth, a common bottle neck. They might also implement custom int8 quantization and dequantization kernels and tune their code for the unique memory layout of edge-class GPUs to enable appli cations like autonomous drones and self-driving cars. An algorithms researcher developing a novel architecture might need custom CUDA to demonstrate competitive performance. Although many new operations can be com posed from existing PyTorch primitives, some genuinely require custom implemen tations. The FlashAttention paper ( https: / /arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135 ), for example, required custom CUDA to achieve its memory efficiency gains.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Even if a model can write a kernel that beats what most expert kernel engineers would produce, someone still has to understand that kernel before it ships. Gener ated kernels are unusually verifiable in isolation: you can compare outputs against a reference, inspect intermediates, and benchmark on fixed shapes, and good work flows do all of that. But a test suite only tells you that the kernel passed the checks you thought to write. A reduction reordered in a way that loses precision, or an accu mulation done in the wrong data type, can slip through and surface later as slightly wrong activations and the wrong tokens coming out of a production model. Trusting code you cannot read is not an engineering strategy. This book gives you the building blocks to open a fast machine-generated kernel and reason about the optimizations inside it: why the tiling is shaped that way, what the memory access pattern costs, and where the arithmetic can drift.

regions.text: VRAM stands for video RAM . As the name suggests, it was originally designed to hold video and graphics data. Think of the massive textures, complex 3D models, and lighting information needed to render a realistic scene in a video game. These are all just large arrays of numbers that need to be processed in parallel to update the mil lions of pixels on your screen many times per second.

regions.label: text
regions.text: It turns out that the mathematical operations used in graphics, such as multiplying matrices to transform 3D coordinates and applying filters to textures, are strikingly similar to the operations at the heart of deep learning, such as matrix multiplications in dense layers and convolutions for image processing. The hardware architecture built to accelerate graphics, with its thousands of simple cores for parallel process ing, was perfectly suited to the massive, parallel computations required to train and run neural networks. So the “video” RAM became the workhorse for AI.

regions.text: A CPU has a few complex cores with large caches, built to run one thread of sequen tial, branchy code as fast as possible. A 16-core desktop CPU such as AMD’s Ryzen 9 9950X3D runs at up to 5.7 GHz, and each core can do two 512-bit fused multiply-adds per clock, 32 FP32 multiply-adds in all. The RTX 3090 used in this book has 10,496 far simpler CUDA cores at a 1.7 GHz boost clock, each doing one FP32 multiply-add per clock. In total, the GPU peaks at about 35.6 TFLOPS of FP32, while the CPU stays under 6 TFLOPS even if all 16 cores held 5.7 GHz. GPU cores are built to execute the same instruction on different data simultaneously. As illustrated in figure 1.1, this tradeoff is visible in how chip real estate is allocated: GPUs devote far more silicon to arithmetic logic units (the cores) and less to cache and control flow units than CPUs do.

As we see in figure 1.1, this design enables GPUs to excel at parallel tasks where the same operation is performed on different data simultaneously. These two worlds must communicate and coordinate. Because the host and device have separate memory spaces, you need to explicitly manage data movement between them: allocating GPU memory, copying data to the device, running your kernel, and copying results back. Your host code orchestrates this workflow. Figure 1.2 illustrates this four-step data flow pattern that every CUDA program follows.

regions.text: Computer scientists call this pattern SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data). It’s one of the four categories in Flynn’s taxonomy, the standard classification of proces sor architectures ( https: / /doi.org/10.1109/TC.1972.5009071 ). GPUs use a closely related model called SIMT: Single Instruction, Multiple Threads. The distinction matters: in pure SIMD, every lane executes the same instruction in lockstep, with no ability to diverge. SIMT also runs thousands of threads on the same instruction, but individual threads can branch independently, and the hardware handles divergence transparently. For the data-parallel patterns we care about in deep learning, the effect is similar to SIMD, but SIMT gives us more flexibility when control flow varies across threads.

regions.text: CUDA —NVIDIA released CUDA in 2007, and it immediately found adoption in high-performance computing (HPC) and scientific computing. Researchers in physics simulations, computational fluid dynamics, and financial modeling were among the first to use GPUs for general-purpose computation. The pro gramming model that CUDA introduced—writing C-like code that runs on thou sands of parallel threads—opened up GPU hardware to applications far beyond graphics.

This pro cess involves similar patterns of parallel arithmetic, computing these derivatives for millions of parameters simultaneously. ¡ Attention mechanisms —A key innovation in modern transformers, attention com putes the relationships between every pair of tokens in a sequence. This requires a number of dot products that scales quadratically with sequence length, but for tunately, all of these dot products can be computed in parallel. These operations contain massive parallelism. Element-wise operations like activations are truly independent: each output depends on exactly one input. Matrix multiplica tions and convolutions require some coordination (each output element is a reduction over many inputs), but the sheer number of output elements still provides abundant parallel work. GPUs thrive on this pattern.

GPUs thrive on this pattern.

regions.text: 1.6.3 The compounding effect When you combine memory optimizations, tensor cores, kernel fusion, and quanti zation, the improvements compound. Each technique builds on the others. A naive implementation versus a fully optimized one can differ by multiple orders of magni tude in both speed and memory efficiency. Quantization together with Flash Attention, which avoids storing large intermediate matrices, lets you run substantially larger models on the same hardware. The optimization stack in this book addresses the following: ¡ Throughput —Faster token generation during inference ¡ Memory efficiency —Fitting larger models or longer sequence contexts ¡ Training cost —Completing runs in less time with fewer GPUs ¡ Latency —Reducing time to first token for interactive applications

regions.label: footer
regions.text: 1.6.4 Scaling to multiple GPUs Everything covered so far focuses on single-GPU optimization. Chapter 10 extends these techniques to multi-GPU setups. Different interconnects have vastly different bandwidths. GPUs connected by NVLink communicate far faster than GPUs con nected over PCIe. Master the single-GPU techniques first. The optimization skills from chapters 5 through 9 transfer directly to distributed scenarios, where inefficiencies multiply with each GPU you add.

regions.label: footer
regions.text: 1.6.5 Why this matters By the end of this book, you’ll understand when and why custom kernels can outper form library implementations. You’ll see why Flash Attention was a breakthrough and how quantization enables deployment scenarios that would otherwise be impractical. Most importantly, you’ll think like a performance engineer: someone who can identify computational bottlenecks and systematically address them.

regions.label: footer
regions.text: 1.7 Getting ready to build Before we continue, a note on terminology: “CUDA” refers to the entire ecosystem, not just the C++ programming model. This includes CUDA C++ (what we’ll write), cuBLAS (optimized linear algebra), cuDNN (DL primitives), CUTLASS (template library), Thrust (parallel algorithms), and more. PyTorch’s heaviest operations, such as matrix multiply and convolution, dispatch to cuBLAS and cuDNN, though PyTorch also ships many handwritten CUDA kernels of its own. This book focuses on CUDA

For this book, a GPU with compute capability 7.0 or later (V100, or any RTX 20-series card and newer) is enough to follow chapters 2 through 6, which cover the core programming model, neural- network building blocks, and profiling. The current CUDA 13 toolchain no longer compiles for older architectures such as Pascal. Chapters 7 and 8 (tensor cores and Flash Attention) require a GPU with tensor cores, meaning the RTX 20 series (Turing) or newer; some of the chapter 11 CUTLASS examples target the same hardware. The distributed material in chapter 10 is written as an advanced case study, so a single GPU is fine for understanding the concepts, even though the measured runs use an 8× GPU server. Data center GPUs (V100, A100, H100, B200) work great if you have access to them, but no chapter strictly requires one. You’ll need the CUDA Toolkit, which provides the nvcc compiler; NVIDIA drivers, which you can verify with nvidia-smi ; and a Python environment. I use uv for Python package management. For operating systems, Linux provides the smoothest experience. On Windows, NVIDIA ships a native CUDA Toolkit and also actively supports CUDA inside WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux), which is the closest match to the Linux workflow used in this book. Detailed installation instructions are provided in appendix A. The beauty is that you can start with basic tools and add advanced profiling and multi-GPU capabilities as you progress through the book. regions.text: Summary ¡ GPUs excel at throughput by running the same instruction across massive data sets in parallel, making them ideal for deep learning workloads. ¡ Host code (CPU) orchestrates work while device code (GPU) executes it. Every CUDA project involves explicit memory transfers between CPU RAM and GPU memory. ¡ CUDA launches thousands of threads organized into grids and blocks. Each thread computes a unique index to determine which data element it processes. ¡ Matrix multiplications, convolutions, activations, and attention computations all fit the “same operation, different data” pattern. Recognizing these opportunities is the first skill of a CUDA performance engineer.

regions.text: Latency is about how fast you can complete a single task. Think of a Formula 1 car. It’s built to get one person from point A to point B at blistering speed. CPUs are latency-optimized machines. They have a few incredibly powerful cores designed to execute complex, sequential instructions as quickly as possi ble. This is perfect for tasks like loading a web page or responding to a mouse click.

regions.text: Deep learning is a throughput problem. We don’t care about doing one multiplication super fast; we care about doing billions of them. A single GPU operation has more startup overhead than a CPU instruction, but once running, the GPU processes vastly more data per second. That tradeoff defines the entire programming model we’re about to learn. A GPU core is a collection of simple execution units. The most important of these is the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU). An ALU is a digital circuit that performs basic math and logic operations; think add , multiply , and , and or . A single CPU core has very sophisti cated ALUs and a lot of complex control logic around them. A GPU core is much sim pler and is often just a handful of ALUs designed for floating-point and integer math. The magic is that a single CUDA thread you write in your code will be scheduled to run on one of these hardware cores. When you launch thousands of threads, you are effectively lighting up thousands of these simple ALUs to perform their calculations at the same time. We’ll revisit the deeper architecture of streaming multiprocessors (SMs) as we need it in later chapters, but for now, remember the contrast: a CPU thread is a heavyweight, OS-managed context, whereas a CUDA thread is a lightweight, hard ware-managed lane scheduled in groups on the GPU. That difference is why we can launch thousands of CUDA threads without the overhead you’d expect on the CPU.

The numbers inside tell the GPU how many parallel workers to launch. In this case, we’re launching 8 threads. What’s a thread? A thread is a single instance of our kernel function running on a GPU core. By launching 8 threads, we tell the GPU to run our vectorAdd function 8 times simultaneously. regions.text: The 8-thread example is great for learning, but what happens when we want to process a million elements? A single block can only hold a limited number of threads (typically 1,024). To go bigger, we need to launch multiple blocks.

regions.text: Think of it like an apartment complex. The grid is the entire complex. Each block is a single floor. Each thread is a single room on that floor. To find a specific room, you need to know its floor number ( blockIdx.x ) and its room number on that floor ( threadIdx.x ).

regions.label: text
regions.text: Figure 2.2 shows the hierarchy as a 2D grid so you can see multiple blocks at once. We’re still working with a 1D row of data in this chapter, but the same indexing princi ples apply. The specific block and thread numbers in this figure (and in figures 2.3 and 2.4) are there to illustrate the layout. The order in which blocks actually run is sched uled by the hardware and is not guaranteed to be the same across GPUs, so never write a kernel that depends on it.

regions.label: number
regions.text: Figure 2.2 CUDA organizes parallel execution into a two-level hierarchy. Threads are the smallest unit of execution and are grouped into blocks. Blocks are then organized into a grid. Each thread has a unique ID within its block ( threadIdx ), and each block has a unique ID within the grid ( blockIdx ). Combined with the block size ( blockDim ), these indices let every thread compute a globally unique position to process.

regions.text: And our kernel needs to use the full global index formula. But there’s one more catch. If n isn't perfectly divisible by threadsPerBlock , we’ll launch more threads than we have elements. For example, if n = 1,000 and threadsPerBlock = 256 , we’ll launch 4 blocks, for a total of 4 * 256 = 1024 threads. The last 24 threads would try to access memory outside the valid range. To prevent this, we add a simple boundary check , shown in figure 2.3.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Figure 2.3 When the total number of elements is not evenly divisible by the block size, CUDA launches extra threads beyond the valid data range. The shaded region shows threads whose computed index exceeds the array bounds. Each thread must check whether its index is valid before accessing memory; threads outside the bounds simply return early without doing any work. This boundary check prevents illegal memory accesses that would otherwise crash the program or corrupt data.

regions.text: Figure 2.4 For 3D data, such as volumetric images or batched 2D tensors, CUDA supports 3D grids of 3D blocks. Each thread identifies its position using six built-in variables: blockIdx in x, y, and z for the block’s position in the grid, and threadIdx in x, y, and z for the thread’s position within its block. The total number of threads per block (x times y times z) must not exceed 1,024 on most GPUs.

Our thread block covers the spatial and channel dimensions, and each thread loops over the batch dimension to linearize that 4D structure into the 1D memory layout that PyTorch, NumPy, and CUDA all use by default (row-major order). Keep in mind that this per-thread batch loop is a deliberate simplification: it serializes the batch, so a thread performs batch_size iter ations one after another. For a large batch, you would instead map the batch onto a grid dimension (for example, folding batch and channels together into blockIdx.z ) so those images are processed in parallel rather than in a loop.

regions.text: Summary ¡ A CUDA program consists of two main parts: host code that runs on the CPU and orchestrates the process and device code (kernels) that runs in massively parallel threads on the GPU. ¡ The terms host and device are the official CUDA terminology for the CPU and GPU, respectively. They have separate memory spaces. ¡ Data must be explicitly transferred between host (RAM) and device (VRAM) memory using cudaMemcpy . This transfer is a potential performance bottleneck. ¡ GPU memory is managed with cudaMalloc and cudaFree , analogous to C’s malloc and free for host memory. ¡ A kernel is a C++ function marked with global that is launched from the host and executed by many threads on the device. ¡ CUDA organizes threads into a two-level hierarchy: threads are grouped into blocks , and blocks are organized into a grid . ¡ Each thread calculates a unique global index using built-in variables ( blockIdx , threadIdx , blockDim , and gridDim ) to determine which piece of data it is respon sible for processing. ¡ Essential C concepts like pointers ( * ) are fundamental to CUDA, as they are used to manage memory addresses on both the host and device. ¡ A simple CUDA program can be compiled from the command line using the CUDA compiler ( nvcc ).

After we run our fancy new GPU kernel, our very last step will always be to compare its output, element by element, to the output of our trusted CPU version. If they match, we can proceed with confidence. If not, we know exactly where the problem is.

regions.text: The two nested for loops in the CPU code are the perfect target for parallelization. Instead of having a single CPU core iterate through every row and column one by one, we can launch a 2D grid of GPU threads. Each thread in this grid is responsible for a single (row, column) pair, effectively executing one iteration of the loop pair in parallel with all other threads.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Matrix transposition is a fundamental data reshaping operation. It flips a matrix over its diagonal, so an element at (row, col) moves to (col, row) . This might seem simple, but it’s essential in deep learning. For instance, when a convolutional neural network (CNN) 2D feature map needs to be flattened and fed into a dense layer, or when atten tion mechanisms in Transformers need to align query and key matrices for multipli cation, transposition is the tool for the job. It allows us to rearrange data to meet the specific dimensional requirements of different network layers. Figure 3.2 shows how a transpose swaps rows and columns.

regions.label: text
regions.text: We parallelize the two outer for loops. Each thread is assigned a unique (row, column) pair in the output matrix C . This means the thread is responsible for computing one full dot product. The innermost for loop, the dot product itself, is still performed by each thread individually. This is a good parallelization strategy because the computa tion of each output element is completely independent of the others.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Softmax is a normalization method used across neural networks, from the final layer of classifiers to attention mechanisms in large language models. Its purpose is to take a vec tor of arbitrary real-valued scores (called logits ) and transform them into a probability distribution, where each element is between 0 and 1 and all elements sum to 1. This naive version is highly inefficient because it involves redundant calculations, but it’s an excel lent way to understand the data-dependent nature of reduction operations on a GPU.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Our naive CUDA kernel, shown in listing 3.12, parallelizes this process by assigning one thread to each output element. The major inefficiency is that, to calculate its sin gle output value, each thread must first read its entire row twice: once to find the maxi mum value and again to find the sum of exponentials. This means all threads working on the same row perform the same redundant reads and calculations. We will fix this with more advanced techniques later.

regions.label: text
regions.text: 3.3.1 Kernel 4, 1D convolution: Processing signals and sequences

regions.label: text
regions.text: 1D convolution is a cornerstone of signal processing and is used in deep learning to pro cess sequential data such as time series or text. The operation works by sliding a small filter (the kernel) across an input signal. At each position, it computes a dot product between the filter and the segment of the input it currently overlaps. This process extracts features, such as patterns or trends, from the local neighborhood of each point in the signal.

regions.label: text
regions.text: NOTE Strictly speaking, the operation we implement here (and in the 2D case that follows) is cross-correlation , not the mathematical convolution from signal processing, because we do not flip the filter before applying it. Deep learning frameworks such as PyTorch and TensorFlow do the same thing and still call it “convolution,” so we follow that convention throughout the book. Since the filter weights are learned, the missing flip makes no difference to what the network can represent.

regions.label: text
regions.text: 2D convolution is the fundamental operation of CNNs. It works just like its 1D cousin but operates on 2D data, such as images. A small 2D filter (e.g., 3 × 3 or 5 × 5) slides over the input image. At each position, the output pixel is the dot product of the filter

regions.label: text
regions.text: 2D convolution is the fundamental operation of CNNs. It works just like its 1D cousin but operates on 2D data, such as images. A small 2D filter (e.g., 3 × 3 or 5 × 5) slides over the input image. At each position, the output pixel is the dot product of the filter and the patch of the image it covers. This allows the network to learn to detect sim ple features such as edges, corners, and textures, which are then combined by deeper layers into more complex object representations. Figure 3.3 illustrates how different filters can detect different features in an image.

regions.text: As before, we parallelize the two outer loops. In the CUDA kernel shown in listing 3.18, each thread is assigned an (output_row, output_col) coordinate and is responsible for computing the value of that single output pixel by performing the two inner loops over the kernel. Figure 3.4 shows the sliding-window operation in detail.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Max pooling is a downsampling operation commonly used in CNNs, typically after a convolutional layer. Its purpose is twofold: it reduces the spatial dimensions (height and width) of the feature maps, which makes the network more computationally efficient, and it provides a degree of translation invariance, meaning the network becomes less sensitive to the exact location of a feature in the image. It works by sliding a window (e.g., 2 × 2) over the input and, for each window, outputting only the maximum value. Figure 3.5 illustrates this downsampling process with a stride of 1, so consecutive windows overlap and a 3 × 3 input produces a 2 × 2 output; one thread computes each output value. Note that the implementation we write next uses the more common configuration, where the stride equals the window size, so the windows tile the input without overlapping and each dimension shrinks by the pool factor.

regions.text: And with that, let’s pause for a moment to take a breath. We’ve just implemented the fundamental building blocks for a huge variety of neural networks, entirely from scratch in CUDA. More importantly, we have dissected the single most important part of writing correct kernels: mapping a thread’s abstract ID to a concrete memory loca tion. Calculating a global index and using it to access data is the foundation of all GPU programming.

regions.text: These kernels are indeed reference implementations: they produce the same numerical output as their optimized counterparts, but they run tens to hundreds of times slower than production libraries like cuDNN and cuBLAS. Still, they embody the exact logic at the core of real neural networks. The gemm_kernel we wrote performs the same computation as a Linear layer. Our softmax_kernel normalizes logits the same way a classifier does. And the conv2d_kernel and maxpool2d_kernel match the operations inside CNNs, which we will continue investigating in this book.

Still, they embody the exact logic at the core of real neural networks. The gemm_kernel we wrote performs the same computation as a Linear layer. Our softmax_kernel normalizes logits the same way a classifier does. And the conv2d_kernel and maxpool2d_kernel match the operations inside CNNs, which we will continue investigating in this book.

regions.text: Summary ¡ Every kernel starts with a simple, slow CPU version that serves as the gold stan dard. Only after the GPU output matches the CPU output element by element do we move on to performance tuning. ¡ Transpose, GEMM, softmax, convolution, and pooling can all be written in 10 to 25 lines of CUDA. These kernels are tens to hundreds of times slower than cuDNN and cuBLAS, but they are complete, understandable, and debuggable. ¡ A transpose implemented as out[col * rows + row] = in[row * cols + col] works but immediately exposes a performance cliff: the reads from in are coalesced (consecutive threads touch consecutive addresses), while the writes to out are strided and therefore noncoalesced. The standard fix (staging a tile through shared memory with padding so both the reads and writes are coalesced) is left as an exercise here; we spend our optimization budget in chapter 6 on the kernels most central to transformer inference. ¡ Reductions are data dependent. Softmax requires two passes over each row (max and sum), which naively leads to every thread in the row recomputing the same values. This redundancy is exactly what we eliminate in chapter 6, where a block per- row strategy and the online-softmax algorithm turn this naive version into a heavily optimized one. ¡ 1D, 2D, and 3D convolutions share the same loop structure: an outer loop over output positions and an inner loop (or loops) over the filter. Pooling is identical, except the inner loop performs max instead of multiply-accumulate. ¡ Once you can launch a grid of threads and compute the correct index, you can express any per-element, per-row, or per-window operation found in modern deep learning frameworks.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Summary ¡ Every kernel starts with a simple, slow CPU version that serves as the gold stan dard. Only after the GPU output matches the CPU output element by element do we move on to performance tuning. ¡ Transpose, GEMM, softmax, convolution, and pooling can all be written in 10 to 25 lines of CUDA. These kernels are tens to hundreds of times slower than cuDNN and cuBLAS, but they are complete, understandable, and debuggable. ¡ A transpose implemented as out[col * rows + row] = in[row * cols + col] works but immediately exposes a performance cliff: the reads from in are coalesced (consecutive threads touch consecutive addresses), while the writes to out are strided and therefore noncoalesced. The standard fix (staging a tile through shared memory with padding so both the reads and writes are coalesced) is left as an exercise here; we spend our optimization budget in chapter 6 on the kernels most central to transformer inference. ¡ Reductions are data dependent. Softmax requires two passes over each row (max and sum), which naively leads to every thread in the row recomputing the same values. This redundancy is exactly what we eliminate in chapter 6, where a block per- row strategy and the online-softmax algorithm turn this naive version into a heavily optimized one. ¡ 1D, 2D, and 3D convolutions share the same loop structure: an outer loop over output positions and an inner loop (or loops) over the filter. Pooling is identical, except the inner loop performs max instead of multiply-accumulate. ¡ Once you can launch a grid of threads and compute the correct index, you can express any per-element, per-row, or per-window operation found in modern deep learning frameworks.

regions.label: number
regions.text: 4.1 Level 1: The PyTorch approach In our journey from high-level frameworks to bare-metal CUDA, we need a reliable point of reference: a “gold standard” against which we can verify every subsequent implementation. For this, we turn to PyTorch. Its combination of a high-level API, automatic differentiation, and highly optimized, battle-tested backend libraries makes it the perfect candidate for our trusted implementation.

regions.label: text
regions.text: In our journey from high-level frameworks to bare-metal CUDA, we need a reliable point of reference: a “gold standard” against which we can verify every subsequent implementation. For this, we turn to PyTorch. Its combination of a high-level API, automatic differentiation, and highly optimized, battle-tested backend libraries makes it the perfect candidate for our trusted implementation.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The goal in this section is to build a PyTorch model in a way that is reproducible and comparable to our future low-level versions. This PyTorch implementation will be our benchmark for correctness (does it converge to a similar loss curve?) and performance. One caveat up front: each version in this chapter initializes its weights with a differ ent random number generator (PyTorch, then NumPy, then C’s rand() ), so the exact per-epoch loss values will not match across implementations. The C and CUDA versions even seed from the clock, so they change from run to run. What we are checking is that every version trains, drives the loss down at a comparable rate, and reaches a similar final accuracy, not that they print identical numbers. The full code for this section is in the v1.py script.

regions.label: text
regions.text: First, we import the necessary libraries, define the hyperparameters, and load the dataset from preprocessed binary files. These binary files (X_train.bin, y_train. bin, etc.) are generated by the v0.py script, which is available in the book’s source code repository. This script handles downloading, normalizing, and converting the MNIST dataset, providing a common data foundation for all our implementations. We will load this data directly into GPU memory, bypassing the typical DataLoader pipeline.

regions.label: abstract
regions.text: The MLP architecture is defined in a standard PyTorch nn.Module . A critical step in our verification process is to override PyTorch’s default weight initialization with a man ual Kaiming He initialization (also called He initialization). This weight initialization scheme, named after researcher Kaiming He, helps prevent vanishing and exploding gradients during training by scaling initial weights based on layer size. Using the same initialization scheme in all our implementations ensures that the PyTorch, NumPy, C, and CUDA versions all start from the same weight distribution. The actual weight val ues differ because each language draws from a different random number generator, but the loss curves should closely track one another, which is what we need for compar ison. The model definition and initialization are shown in the following listing.

regions.text: With the model initialized, we need a training loop that not only trains the model but also carefully times each distinct step of the process. The train_timed function in listing 4.3 is designed for this purpose. It iterates through the data and records the time spent on data loading, the forward pass, loss computation, the backward pass, and the optimizer’s weight updates. This level of detail is crucial for identifying performance bottlenecks later on.

regions.text: At its core, backpropagation is an elegant application of the chain rule from calcu lus. Imagine a simple chain of calculations: an input x is passed to a function g to pro duce y , and y is then passed to a function f to produce the final result z . The chain rule allows us to find how a small change in x affects z by multiplying the sensitivities of each step along the chain. This concept is the key to training neural networks. We have a loss function L that depends on the network’s output, which in turn depends on many layers of functions involving weights and inputs. The chain rule lets us calculate how any given weight affects the final loss by propagating the gradient backward from the loss, one step at a time.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The forward pass of a linear layer is a matrix multiplication, Y = XW + b , where X is the input, W is the weight matrix, and b is the bias vector. To add a vector b to a matrix XW, we use broadcasting: the bias vector is added to each row of the output matrix. If X has shape (batch_size, input_dim) and W has shape (input_dim, output_dim), then XW produces a matrix of shape (batch_size, output_dim), and the bias b , with shape (output_dim,), is added element-wise to each of those rows.

regions.text: As illustrated in figure 4.7, if a neuron’s input Z during the forward pass is positive, the gate is open, and the gradient passes through unchanged (indicated by the arrows). If the input is negative, the gate is closed, and the gradient is blocked (becomes 0). This is implemented as an element-wise multiplication: dL/dZ = dL/dA * (Z > 0) , where (Z > 0) creates a binary mask that is 1 for positive values and 0 for negative values.

regions.text: 4.2.4 Common pitfalls and debugging tips When implementing backpropagation manually, several common problems can arise. The most frequent error is getting matrix dimensions wrong. Always ensure that the shapes of your gradients match the shapes of the parameters or inputs they corre spond to. During training, monitor the magnitude of your gradients. If they become exces sively large (exploding) or excessively small (vanishing), they can destabilize or stall the learning process. A simple utility function, shown in the following listing, can help track the norm and maximum value of gradients to detect these problems early.

regions.label: number
regions.text: def check_gradients(gradients, name): for param_name, grad in gradients.items(): grad_norm = np.linalg.norm(grad) grad_max = np.max(np.abs(grad)) print(f"{name} - {param_name}: norm={grad_norm:.6f}, max={grad_max:.6f}")

regions.text: 4.2.5 Vectorized implementation for batches For efficiency, we process multiple samples (a batch) at once. The forward pass natu rally handles this through matrix multiplication. The backward pass requires careful handling of the batch dimension. The key difference, as shown in listing 4.7, is that we use NumPy’s advanced indexing to subtract 1 from the correct class position for every sample in the batch simultaneously. The weight gradients then naturally accumulate the contributions from all samples.

regions.text: 4.3 Level 3: The NumPy approach Now that we have our PyTorch gold standard, we take our first step down the abstrac tion ladder by reimplementing the entire training pipeline in NumPy. This forces us to manually implement every mathematical operation: the forward pass, the activa tion functions, the cross-entropy loss, and, most importantly, the entire backpropaga tion algorithm. Previously, we explored automatic differentiation theory through the computational graph in section 4.2.1 and relied on PyTorch’s .backward() method; now we put that theory into practice. This NumPy version serves two critical purposes. First, it’s a direct, code-based application of the backpropagation theory we’ve discussed. Second, it acts as an essential debugging bridge between the “magic” of autograd and the explicit, low level logic we’ll need for C and CUDA. If our NumPy implementation drives the loss down at the same rate and reaches a similar final accuracy as our PyTorch implemen tation (recall that the exact per-epoch numbers differ because the two use different random initializations), we can be much more confident that our understanding of the underlying mathematics is correct. The full code for this section is in the v2.py script.

regions.label: text
regions.text: This NumPy version serves two critical purposes. First, it’s a direct, code-based application of the backpropagation theory we’ve discussed. Second, it acts as an essential debugging bridge between the “magic” of autograd and the explicit, low level logic we’ll need for C and CUDA. If our NumPy implementation drives the loss down at the same rate and reaches a similar final accuracy as our PyTorch implemen tation (recall that the exact per-epoch numbers differ because the two use different random initializations), we can be much more confident that our understanding of the underlying mathematics is correct. The full code for this section is in the v2.py script.

regions.text: With these building blocks, we can construct the NeuralNetwork class, shown in list ing 4.9. This class holds the model’s weights and biases and defines the forward and backward passes. Figure 4.8 visualizes the data flow for these passes. To manually imple ment backpropagation, we must explicitly manage the intermediate results from the forward pass. The forward method doesn’t just return the final output; it also returns a cache containing the inputs and activation outputs from each layer. This cache is then passed to the backward method, which uses these stored values to calculate the gradi ents for each weight and bias correctly according to the chain rule. The final step in training is updating the weights. Once we have the gradients, we adjust each weight by taking a step in the direction opposite of its gradient. The size of this step is controlled by the learning_rate hyperparameter. A smaller learning rate means smaller, more cautious steps toward the minimum loss, while a larger learning rate takes bigger steps but risks overshooting. This weight-update step, com bined with the forward and backward passes, completes one iteration of the training loop.

A smaller learning rate means smaller, more cautious steps toward the minimum loss, while a larger learning rate takes bigger steps but risks overshooting. This weight-update step, com bined with the forward and backward passes, completes one iteration of the training loop. regions.text: 4.3.2 Verification technique: Isolate and conquer

regions.label: text
regions.text: To check our manual implementation, we use a debugging approach called: Isolate and Conquer. When a complex system breaks, the most effective strategy is to chop it into smaller, testable pieces. Instead of debugging the whole training loop, we verify each component individually against our trusted PyTorch model.

regions.label: text
regions.text: We can load the exact same initial weights into both models, pass the same single batch of data through them, and assert that the output of each layer is numerically identical. The following listing shows how we could write a simple test to verify our first linear layer and ReLU activation in NumPy against the PyTorch equivalent.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Moving from NumPy to C takes us another step closer to the hardware. Here, we lose the convenience of NumPy’s high-level array operations and must implement every thing from scratch. The C version, found in v3.c, is a direct, line-by-line translation of the logic we developed in NumPy. Its purpose is not speed, but to serve as an explicit, low-level blueprint for the CUDA implementation to come.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Unlike Python, C requires manual memory management. We must explicitly allocate memory for every component of our network using malloc . The initialize_neural_ network function in listing 4.14 handles this by allocating space for all weights and gradients. It then calls helper functions to initialize the weights with our standard He initialization and the biases to zero. This explicit control over memory will be central to our work in CUDA.

regions.text: 4.4.3 The forward pass in C The forward pass requires us to implement each mathematical operation manually. The most computationally intensive part is matrix multiplication, which we implement with three nested loops, as shown in the matmul_a_b function in listing 4.15. The func tion performs the operation C = A @ B , where matrix A has shape (m, n) , matrix B has shape (n, k) , and the result C has shape (m, k) . The parameters m , n , and k therefore define the dimensions of the matrices involved. We also need explicit loops for adding the bias and applying the ReLU activation. These handwritten loops are the exact com putations we will later parallelize in CUDA.

regions.label: number
regions.text: Listing 4.15 C forward pass operations

regions.label: number
regions.text: void matmul_a_b(float *A, float *B, float *C, int m, int n, int k) { for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) { for (int j = 0; j < k; j++) { C[i * k + j] = 0.0f; for (int l = 0; l < n; l++) { C[i * k + j] += A[i * n + l] * B[l * k + j]; } } } }

regions.label: text
regions.text: We now arrive at the core of this chapter: translating our C implementation into a par allel version using CUDA. The goal of this first “naive” implementation is correctness, not performance. We will take the explicit loops from our C functions and convert them, one by one, into simple CUDA kernels. This direct translation provides a func tional GPU-based MLP and a solid foundation on which we will build optimizations in later chapters.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The full implementation is in v4.cu. It mirrors the structure of v3.c but uses host functions that launch GPU kernels instead of executing CPU loops.

regions.text: The bias_forward_kernel uses a common CUDA pattern for handling batched data. It launches a 1D grid of threads large enough to cover all elements in the x tensor ( batch_size * size ). Each thread computes a unique linear index, idx . It then decom poses this linear index back into a 2D coordinate: the batch index b = idx / size and the feature index i = idx % size . This allows each thread to identify its target element in the batch and add the corresponding bias term, bias[i] .

regions.label: text
regions.text: The compute_output_gradients_kernel is launched with a 1D grid where each thread is responsible for one sample in the batch. The thread then calculates the gradient for its corresponding output vector by subtracting 1 from the correct class logit. The bias_backward_kernel demonstrates a parallel reduction. Each thread is assigned to a single bias term ( i ). It then iterates through all samples in the batch ( for (int b = 0; b < batch_size; b++) ) to sum up the gradients that correspond to its assigned bias. This is a naive reduction; we will see much more efficient ways to do this later.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The training loop now orchestrates kernel launches instead of function calls. For each batch, it first copies the input data and labels from the host to the device using cudaMemcpy , then calls the forward, backward, and weight update functions, which in turn launch their respective GPU kernels. A key difference is the need for synchroniza tion. Since kernel launches are asynchronous, we must call cudaDeviceSynchronize() after each kernel, as in the following listing, to ensure its computation is complete before we time it.

regions.text: Look closely at that softmax launch: <<<batch_size, 1>>> puts one thread in each block, so each block occupies a full 32-thread warp with 31 lanes idle, and the whole launch keeps only a tiny fraction of the GPU busy. We accept that here because the output layer is just 10 values wide per sample, and our goal is a correct translation, but this is exactly the kind of launch configuration that profiling flags immediately. Chapter 6 shows how to structure reductions like softmax so a full block cooperates on each row. The backward pass follows a similar pattern but in reverse order. We start by comput ing the output gradients from the softmax and cross-entropy loss, then propagate these gradients backward through each layer. Each gradient computation requires the inter mediate values cached during the forward pass, which is why we must carefully manage

regions.text: A critical concept in CUDA development is understanding how to measure perfor mance accurately. Because GPU operations are asynchronous (the CPU launches a ker nel and immediately moves on), using CPU-side timers like clock_gettime() around a block of kernel launches can be misleading. The CPU finishes launching the kernels very quickly, but the GPU may still be working. A final cudaDeviceSynchronize() call then forces the CPU to wait for all GPU work to complete, making that single line appear to take a very long time.

regions.text: 4.5.5 A note on profiling: Wall-clock vs. GPU time A critical concept in CUDA development is understanding how to measure perfor mance accurately. Because GPU operations are asynchronous (the CPU launches a ker nel and immediately moves on), using CPU-side timers like clock_gettime() around a block of kernel launches can be misleading. The CPU finishes launching the kernels very quickly, but the GPU may still be working. A final cudaDeviceSynchronize() call then forces the CPU to wait for all GPU work to complete, making that single line appear to take a very long time. This “wrong timing attribution” is a common pitfall. The correct way to measure the time a kernel takes on the GPU is with CUDA Events. By recording an event before and after a kernel launch and then calculating the elapsed time between them, we can get a precise measurement of the GPU’s execution time, separate from any CPU or mem ory transfer overhead. The following listing shows a simple timing utility using CUDA Events.

regions.label: number

regions.label: number
regions.text: cudaEventRecord(start); my_kernel<<<grid, block>>>(args); // kernel to time cudaEventRecord(stop); cudaEventSynchronize(stop); float milliseconds = 0; cudaEventElapsedTime(&milliseconds, start, stop); printf("Kernel time: %.3f ms\n", milliseconds); cudaEventDestroy(start); cudaEventDestroy(stop);

regions.text: The core of the optimization is replacing our manual matrix multiplication kernels with calls to cublasSgemm . Listing 4.29 shows the forward pass, now using cublasSgemm for both linear layers. Note that the other operations, such as adding the bias and applying the ReLU activation, are still handled by our custom kernels. This hybrid approach uses NVIDIA’s optimized library for the computationally intensive matrix operations while maintaining control over the simpler element-wise operations.

regions.label: text
regions.text: A critical detail is that cuBLAS, like Fortran and the BLAS libraries it’s based on, assumes matrices are stored in column-major order. C and C++, by contrast, use row- major order. A common and efficient trick for handling this mismatch is to reverse the order of the matrix multiplication ( B @ A instead of A @ B ) and swap the dimensions m and n . This works because (A @ B).T = B.T @ A.T , and transposing a matrix in memory is equivalent to switching its layout from row-major to column-major. Our code uses this trick implicitly, which is why the cublasSgemm calls may look slightly different from the mathematical formulas they represent.

regions.text: CUDAGuard is essential for multi-GPU systems. When you have multiple GPUs, CUDA operations run on the “current” device. If tensor A lives on GPU 1 but the current device is GPU 0, the kernel would launch on the wrong device and crash. The guard sets the current device to match the input tensor and then restores the previous device when the function returns.

regions.label: text
regions.text: ¡ Head —A single attention computation that projects inputs to queries, keys, and values, computes attention scores, and produces an output. Each head learns to focus on different relationships between tokens. ¡ Multihead attention —Multiple heads run in parallel, and their outputs are concatenated and projected back to the model dimension. This allows the model to attend to information from different representation subspaces simultaneously. ¡ Block (or layer) —One complete transformer unit containing multihead attention, a feed-forward network, and the residual connections and layer normalization that wrap them. Our model stacks eight of these blocks. ¡ Model —The complete transformer: token embeddings, position embeddings, a stack of blocks, final layer normalization, and the output projection to vocabu lary logits (the raw, unnormalized scores for each token in the vocabulary before softmax converts them to probabilities).

regions.text: After scaling, we apply a causal mask to enforce autoregressive behavior. The mask is a lower-triangular matrix ( torch.tril ): the lower triangle, including the diago nal, contains ones, and the upper triangle contains zeros. When we mask positions, we set upper-triangle scores to negative infinity before softmax. After exponentiation, these scores become zero probability: position 5 can attend to positions 0–5, but not 6 or beyond. The lower triangle represents the past, or valid attention targets, while the upper triangle represents the future, or forbidden targets. This is what makes the model autoregressive: each prediction depends only on what came before.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The configuration sets up our training dimensions. The 8-layer depth is deliberately chosen to make optimization opportunities visible: inefficiencies that seem minor in shallow models compound significantly as depth increases. With a batch size of 16 and a sequence length of 64, we’re processing 1,024 tokens simultaneously during training, creating abundant parallelism for GPU execution. The embedding dimension of 128 with 4 attention heads means each head operates in a 32-dimensional subspace, bal ancing expressiveness with computational efficiency. In train.py, vocab_size is recom puted from the Wizard of Oz corpus immediately after tokenization. For this dataset, the value is 65, which is why the listing uses that concrete number.

A single attention head computes three projections (query, key, and value) from the input, calculates attention weights between all positions, and applies those weights to the values. The causal mask ensures that each position can attend only to previous posi tions, which is critical for autoregressive language modeling. This inference-oriented head omits the dropout that a training configuration would apply to the attention weights because dropout is inactive at inference time. Each head has its own learned Q, K, and V projection matrices, initialized randomly and updated independently during training. Because each head starts with different weights and receives different gradient signals, they naturally specialize: one might learn to weight adjacent tokens heavily (useful for local syntax), while another might develop broader attention patterns (useful for tracking long-range references like pronouns to their antecedents). This specialization emerges from optimization, not from explicit pro gramming. The following listing shows the multihead attention initialization.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The feed-forward network processes each position independently. It expands to 4× the embedding dimension (128 → 512), applies the GELU activation, and then projects back down. These two layers hold twice as many weights as the attention projections in the same block (2 × 128 × 512 versus 4 × 128 × 128).

regions.label: text
regions.text: Forward execution applies the pre-norm residual pattern twice: normalize, run the sublayer, add the residual, and repeat for the feed-forward layer. Each transformer block has two sublayers: multihead attention (tokens communi cate) and feed-forward (tokens compute independently). Residual connections let gra dients flow directly through the network, and layer normalization stabilizes training. We stack eight of these blocks to create depth. This implementation uses pre-norm order ing: layer norm runs before each sublayer, and the residual add happens afterward. Every operation here is massively parallel: embedding lookups process all tokens simultaneously, attention computes all query-key-value products across the batch in one launch, and feed-forward layers apply the same transformation to every position inde pendently. PyTorch hides this parallelism behind clean abstractions, but underneath, cuBLAS and cuDNN are dispatching thousands of threads per operation. Chapter 6 optimizes the GEMV, softmax, LayerNorm, top-k, and GEMM kernels behind these lay ers, and chapter 8 restructures attention so the full attention matrix never goes to global memory. For now, the PyTorch baseline gives us correctness to validate against and per formance numbers to beat.

Every operation here is massively parallel: embedding lookups process all tokens simultaneously, attention computes all query-key-value products across the batch in one launch, and feed-forward layers apply the same transformation to every position inde pendently. PyTorch hides this parallelism behind clean abstractions, but underneath, cuBLAS and cuDNN are dispatching thousands of threads per operation. Chapter 6 optimizes the GEMV, softmax, LayerNorm, top-k, and GEMM kernels behind these lay ers, and chapter 8 restructures attention so the full attention matrix never goes to global memory. For now, the PyTorch baseline gives us correctness to validate against and per formance numbers to beat.

regions.text: During each generation step, we compute the new token’s key and value vectors and append them to our cache. When computing attention, the new token’s query attends to all cached keys and values, transforming the operation from GEMM (recom puting everything) to GEMV (one query against cached data). Figure 5.7 shows how the cache grows during generation.

regions.text: With KV caching, attention shifts from “full matrix” thinking to the thin column in figure 5.7. Each decode step looks up the new token embedding, adds the positional embedding for the current step, feeds the resulting [B, 1, embed_dim] slice into the cached attention kernels, and appends the new key and value rows to the cache.

regions.text: different learned weights. A router network scores each expert for a given input and selects the top-k experts to run. The term “expert” is a metaphor from the machine learning literature: through training, each network tends to specialize in different input patterns, becoming an “expert” at processing certain types of tokens. This spe cialization emerges from optimization, not from explicit design: the router and experts co-adapt so that tokens get routed to whichever expert produces the best predictions. Figure 5.9 illustrates the MoE architecture.

regions.text: different learned weights. A router network scores each expert for a given input and selects the top-k experts to run. The term “expert” is a metaphor from the machine learning literature: through training, each network tends to specialize in different input patterns, becoming an “expert” at processing certain types of tokens. This spe cialization emerges from optimization, not from explicit design: the router and experts co-adapt so that tokens get routed to whichever expert produces the best predictions. Figure 5.9 illustrates the MoE architecture.

regions.text: MoE allows models to scale to massive parameter counts (trillions) while keeping infer ence costs manageable. Only a handful of experts (top-8 routing is common) out of dozens to hundreds are active per token, dramatically reducing compute requirements. For each token, a router network computes scores for all experts, selects the top-k highest-scoring experts, normalizes their weights, and combines their outputs. During inference, this sparse activation means you compute only a small fraction of the model’s total parameters per token, roughly 3% to 10% in current production models (Deep Seek-V3: 37B of 671B; Qwen3-235B-A22B: 22B of 235B). The routing process involves several key steps:

regions.text: The softmax, top-k selection, and score normalization all run on the GPU, so only the sparse expert dispatch loop runs in Python. This keeps the routing work where mem ory bandwidth is plentiful and trims the number of CPU-GPU tensor dispatches per token down to the handful of experts we actually execute. The CUDA routing imple mentation provides a 1.2 to 1.5× speedup over PyTorch for the MoE model, with the benefits increasing as the number of experts grows. The custom top-k and softmax kernels are particularly effective for this memory-bound routing computation.

regions.text: 5.3.2 GEMV: The inference workhorse Inference turns matrix-matrix multiplication into matrix-vector multiplication. Train ing multiplies a batch of tokens, [B, T, D] @ [D, D] → [B, T, D] , while decode multiplies a single token, [1, 1, D] @ [D, D] → [1, 1, D] . That shift from batch processing to single- token processing requires completely different kernel optimization strategies. The fol lowing comparison shows the difference:

regions.label: number
regions.text: GEMM (training, T=64 tokens): Q[64, 128] @ K.T[128, 64] = Scores[64, 64] -> 64 * 64 * 128 = 524,288 multiply-adds -> High arithmetic intensity, compute-bound

regions.label: number
regions.text: GEMV (inference, 1 new token): q[1, 128] @ K.T[128, 64] = scores[1, 64] -> 1 * 64 * 128 = 8,192 multiply-adds -> Low arithmetic intensity, memory-bound

regions.label: text
regions.text: The top-k kernel identifies the k largest values and their indices for MoE routing. Unlike our previous kernels that parallelize across embedding dimensions or sequence positions, top-k parallelizes across batch elements. Each token in the batch needs its own independent routing decision, so we assign one CUDA block per token. Within each block, a single thread scans through all expert scores and maintains a small sorted buffer of the k best candidates.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The algorithm walks through all n expert scores. For each score, it checks whether the score should enter the top-k buffer by comparing it against the current entries from best to worst. If the score beats an entry, we shift everything below that entry down by one position (evicting the smallest value) and insert the new score. The break state ment ensures that we don’t insert the same score multiple times.

Decode generates tokens one at a time, where each new token depends on all previous tokens. This sequential dependency makes decode GEMV- dominated and memory-bound. ¡ The KV cache stores key and value projections once and reuses them during 2 autoregressive generation, transforming O(N ) recomputation into O(N) as sequences grow. ¡ Training and prefill saturate GPU compute with matrix-matrix multiplication. Decode uses matrix-vector multiplication, where a single query vector multiplies against cached matrices, making memory bandwidth rather than compute the bottleneck. ¡ The GEMV kernel assigns each thread one output element, loads one row of the weight matrix, and computes a dot product with the input vector. Shared memory tiling doesn’t help here because arithmetic intensity is too low: the bot tleneck is memory-read speed, not compute. ¡ MoE replaces a single feed-forward layer with multiple parallel networks. A router scores each expert and selects the top-k experts to execute, so only k/n of the parameters are active per token. This reduces compute while maintaining total model capacity. ¡ Top-k selection for MoE routing uses insertion sort. With small k (typically 2) and small n (8–64 experts), the O(n × k) insertion sort outperforms parallel algo rithms because a single thread scanning 8 values beats the synchronization over

regions.label: text
regions.text: GEMV calculates the product of a matrix and a vector. For transformer inference, par ticularly in an autoregressive setting where we generate one token at a time, the batch size is often just one. In this scenario, the highly parallel nature of GEMM is underuti lized, and the computation effectively becomes a series of GEMV operations. Optimiz ing for this specific case is critical for speeding up how fast tokens stream along the user’s screen.

regions.text: Before we begin optimizing, it’s crucial to understand what makes GEMV different from GEMM. GEMV is a memory-bound operation, meaning performance is limited by how fast we can move data from global memory, not by how fast we can compute.

Divide those FLOPs by the 4-byte loads and stores, and you land near 0.5 FLOPs per byte of traffic.

regions.label: text
regions.text: A warp is the fundamental execution unit on NVIDIA GPUs and consists of exactly 32 threads. These 32 threads execute together in a SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads) fashion: they all execute the same instruction at the same time, but on different data. AMD GPUs have an equivalent concept called a wavefront , which is typically 64 threads wide.

regions.label: text
regions.text: A warp is the fundamental execution unit on NVIDIA GPUs and consists of exactly 32 threads. These 32 threads execute together in a SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads) fashion: they all execute the same instruction at the same time, but on different data. AMD GPUs have an equivalent concept called a wavefront , which is typically 64 threads wide.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The key properties of warps are ¡ Size —Always 32 threads on current NVIDIA GPUs. ¡ Lane ID —Each thread within a warp has a lane ID from 0 to 31, accessible via threadIdx.x % 32 . Lane IDs determine which threads communicate during shuffle operations. ¡ Execution —Threads in a warp execute in lockstep. ¡ Communication —Warp-level primitives like __shfl_down_sync allow threads to exchange data through registers without using shared memory. ¡ Performance —Warp shuffles exchange values directly through registers, avoid ing both the shared-memory round trip and the __syncthreads() barrier that a shared-memory reduction requires, making them faster for reductions within a warp.

regions.text: The GPU’s memory controller fetches data in aligned chunks called cache lines (typi cally 32–128 bytes). When a warp performs a coalesced access to consecutive addresses,

regions.label: text
regions.text: The GPU’s memory controller fetches data in aligned chunks called cache lines (typi cally 32–128 bytes). When a warp performs a coalesced access to consecutive addresses, all 32 threads can be satisfied by just a few cache line reads. When access is uncoalesced with large strides, each thread requires a separate memory transaction. The hardware may have to perform up to 32 separate memory transactions for the 32 threads in a warp, leaving most of each fetched cache line unused.

regions.text: To fix the memory access pattern, we need to fundamentally change our paralleliza tion strategy. Instead of assigning one thread to compute an entire output element,

regions.label: text
regions.text: To fix the memory access pattern, we need to fundamentally change our paralleliza tion strategy. Instead of assigning one thread to compute an entire output element, we’ll assign an entire thread block to compute a single output element. This means that all threads within a block (for example, 32 threads if we launch with a block size of 32) will collaborate on the dot product for a single row.

regions.text: Listing 6.2 shows the warpReduceSum helper function. It uses a loop to progressively sum values across the warp. In each iteration, a thread retrieves the value from the thread whose lane ID is offset higher than its own (for example, lane 0 gets the value from lane 16 when offset is 16). This process halves the number of active threads carry ing partial sums until thread 0 has the total sum.

regions.text: While warp-level shuffles live entirely in registers, it’s worth grounding the concept

regions.label: text
regions.text: While warp-level shuffles live entirely in registers, it’s worth grounding the concept with a recap of a shared-memory reduction. Imagine four threads writing their inputs to shared memory, synchronizing, and then letting the first two threads compare (0,2) and (1,3) . After another barrier, thread 0 compares the survivors to emit the block wide max. That’s all a reduction is: a tree of pairwise combines with __syncthreads() between each level. We’ll use the same tree, just with warp shuffles instead of shared memory when we optimize.

regions.text: Our warp shuffle version is efficient, but it can’t use more than 32 threads per block. To increase parallelism and computational density, we want to use larger thread blocks (e.g., 128, 256, or more threads). To do this, we need a way to reduce values across the entire block, not just within individual warps. This is where shared memory comes in.

regions.text: Figure 6.3 provides the architectural backdrop for this discussion. It shows a streaming multiprocessor (SM) with its warp schedulers, register file, shared memory/L1 cache, and execution units, emphasizing that shared memory sits alongside the schedulers that coordinate those warp-level reductions. We lean on that fast, block- local memory to bridge the gap between warp-level and block-level collaboration.

We lean on that fast, block- local memory to bridge the gap between warp-level and block-level collaboration.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Doubling the active threads means we move twice as much data per iteration, keep more memory requests in flight to cover latency, and give the scheduler room to juggle work instead of idling. In practice, the block-level reduction is about 1.7× faster than the warp-only version, pushing memory bandwidth utilization to roughly 85% to 90% of peak and delivering about 8× the throughput of the naive kernel.

regions.label: text
regions.text: We have successfully addressed memory coalescing, but we can still squeeze more per formance out of our memory operations. Modern GPUs have wide memory buses, and we can saturate this bandwidth more effectively by issuing wider memory loads. Instead of loading one 32-bit float at a time, we can load a 128-bit chunk, which corresponds to four floats. This is called vectorization .

regions.text: We have successfully addressed memory coalescing, but we can still squeeze more per formance out of our memory operations. Modern GPUs have wide memory buses, and we can saturate this bandwidth more effectively by issuing wider memory loads. Instead of loading one 32-bit float at a time, we can load a 128-bit chunk, which corresponds to four floats. This is called vectorization .

regions.label: text
regions.text: CUDA provides built-in vector types like float2 and float4 that map directly to wide load/store instructions. By reinterpreting our float* pointers as float4* pointers, we can direct the compiler to generate these more efficient instructions. This reduces the total number of memory instructions, which can save latency and improve throughput, especially in memory-bound kernels like GEMV. Of course, this technique requires the dimensions of our matrices and vectors to be divisible by the vector size (in this case, 4) and the data to be properly aligned in memory.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Vectorization provides a smaller final boost, on the order of 5% to 10%, because the block-reduction kernel is already close to the bandwidth ceiling. Even so, using float4 loads still helps: it lowers the instruction count because a single load brings in four floats, keeps the memory fabric busy with wider transactions, and signals the compiler to apply vector-friendly rewrites. Together, those effects push bandwidth uti lization to around 97% of peak, matching cuBLAS for GEMV. The total speedup from naive to vectorized is roughly 8x.
