regions.text: The online softmax exploits the multiplication property of exponentials: e^a * e^b = e^(a + b) . When we encounter a new maximum value, we multiply the existing normal ization sum by a correction factor of e^(old_max - new_max) . This rescales all previous contributions to be relative to the new maximum without restarting the computa tion. The correction term ensures numerical correctness while allowing us to fuse two passes into one. This technique is fundamental to Flash Attention, which we’ll explore in chapter 8.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The online algorithm typically provides about a 20% speedup over the naive three-pass approach by reducing global memory reads from 3N to 2N per thread and improving instruction cache locality with fewer loop structures. However, both naive and online implementations still suffer from uncoalesced memory access with threads in a warp reading from different rows, single-thread-per-row limiting parallelism, and no shared memory reuse. The next optimization addresses these fundamental issues by moving to a block-per-row strategy.

Profiling the online softmax kernel with NCU reveals a telling result: despite reduc ing the process from three passes to two, the speedup is modest (around 20%). The occupancy metrics explain why: both the naive and online kernels launch just one thread per row, so the SM stays nearly idle (well under 10% occupancy). regions.label: text
regions.text: The shfl_down_sync instruction exchanges data between threads in a warp using the register file, bypassing shared memory entirely. This provides several benefits. First, there are no shared memory bank conflicts because each thread reads from its own registers. Second, there are no synchronization barriers within warps because warps execute in lockstep. Third, register file access has much lower latency than shared memory access.

regions.label: abstract
regions.text: The fused shared memory kernel delivers dramatic improvements. The memory access pattern is now coalesced because consecutive threads read consecutive elements, the row crosses the global memory bus only twice (once for the online statistics pass, once for normalization), and all cross-thread communication happens in fast on-chip shared memory. Because it puts many threads on each row instead of one, this provides a very large speedup over the naive version, roughly 20× on short rows and over 100× on wide ones, with a similar jump over the online algorithm. The warp shuffle and vectorized refinements that follow bring performance to within a few percent of PyTorch, match ing or slightly beating it.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The online algorithm provides about a 1.2× improvement through algorithmic fusion that reduces passes from 3 to 2. Moving to shared memory with a block-per-row layout

regions.label: text
regions.text: The online algorithm provides about a 1.2× improvement through algorithmic fusion that reduces passes from 3 to 2. Moving to shared memory with a block-per-row layout is the giant step, roughly 90 to 120× at this shape, because it finally parallelizes each row instead of assigning it to a single thread. Warp shuffles add a further ~1.5× by replacing shared-memory reductions with register shuffles, and vectorization adds up to ~15% more at larger N by using float4 loads.

regions.title: The online algorithm provides about a 1.2× improvement through algorithmic fusion that reduces passes from 3 to 2. Moving to shared memory with a block-per-row layout is the giant step, roughly 90 to 120× at this shape, because it finally parallelizes each row instead of assigning it to a single thread. Warp shuffles add a further ~1.5× by replacing shared-memory reductions with register shuffles, and vectorization adds up to ~15% more at larger N by using float4 loads.

regions.label: text
regions.text: This kernel suffers from multiple performance problems. First, uncoalesced mem ory access occurs because each thread processes a different row, with threads 0 and 1 accessing elements N apart, such as x[0] and x[N] , causing strided global memory reads. Second, redundant global memory reads happen because the input row is read three complete times: once for mean calculation, once for variance calculation and once for normalization. For a 1,024-element row, that’s 3,072 global memory reads per thread. Third, there’s no parallelism within rows, as each thread computes seri ally through its entire row. With typical row sizes of 768 to 4,096 elements, this leaves massive parallelism untapped. Fourth, the poor arithmetic intensity means the ratio of computation to memory access is extremely low, making the kernel memory-bound but utilizing memory inefficiently.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Profiling the parallel LayerNorm kernel shows that launching separate kernels for mean, variance, and normalization creates unnecessary global memory traffic. Each kernel reads the entire row from HBM, processes it, and writes results back: three round trips where one would suffice. A fused kernel that keeps the row in shared mem ory throughout all three stages eliminates these redundant transfers.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Assigning one warp of 32 threads to each row is highly efficient for typical transformer hidden dimensions like 768, 1,024, and 2,048. The memory access benefits are substantial: 32 threads load 32 consecutive elements per iteration, achieving perfect coalescing, where each warp’s memory requests combine into one or two cache line reads. For N = 1024 with 32 threads, only 32 iterations are needed, compared with 1,024 serial iterations in the naive version.

regions.label: text
regions.text: reads. For N = 1024 with 32 threads, only 32 iterations are needed, compared with 1,024 serial iterations in the naive version.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Reduction efficiency is excellent because warp shuffle reductions complete in log (32) = 5 dependent steps, five SHFL instructions instead of a shared-memory tree 2 with barriers. No shared memory is needed, eliminating bank conflicts and synchroni zation barriers. __shfl_sync broadcasts the final mean to all lanes instantly.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Our optimization journey for LayerNorm follows three stages. The naive baseline uses thread-per-row with three passes and uncoalesced access. The multikernel parallel approach uses three kernel launches with block-per-row and coalesced access, deliver ing about 7× improvement. The warp-based fused kernel uses a single kernel with warp shuffles, optimal for transformer dimensions, providing roughly 9 to 10× improvement over naive in a single launch.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Our journey now takes us to a kernel that is a cornerstone of mixture-of-experts (MoE) models: top-k. In an MoE transformer, after a “gating” network outputs scores for each available “expert,” the top-k kernel selects the K experts with the highest scores. The input token is then processed only by these selected K experts, which is how MoE mod els achieve massive parameter counts while keeping computation manageable.

regions.label: text
regions.text: A naive way to implement this on a GPU is to use a variation of selection sort. We can launch a single thread (or a single block) that iterates K times. In each iteration, it scans the entire input vector to find the current maximum value that hasn’t already been cho sen, records its value and index, and then marks it as “selected” to avoid picking it again. You can find this implementation in book.cu/4_optim/topK/kernels/0_naive.cu.

regions.label: text
regions.text: This approach is terribly inefficient. The complexity is O(K × N), and it is com pletely sequential. It uses none of the GPU’s massive parallelism. The challenge in parallelizing top-k is that it’s not an easily divisible problem. All threads need to agree on the global top K elements. A more sophisticated approach is needed, typically involving parallel sorting or heap-based algorithms distributed across the threads of a block.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The naive kernel runs K outer-loop iterations, each scanning all N elements to find the next maximum among unselected values. This sequential pattern is inherently difficult to parallelize. The parallel version uses block-wide reductions to find the maximum in each iteration, distributing the search across multiple threads. But the K iterations remain sequential, creating a fundamental bottleneck that limits GPU utilization.

regions.text: NCU profiling of the naive top-k kernel reveals extremely low occupancy: each thread processes an entire row sequentially, leaving most of the SM idle. The kernel is neither compute-bound nor memory-bound; it is simply doing too little parallel work.

regions.text: This algorithm has a much better time complexity of O(N × log(K)), a significant improvement over O(N × K). We can implement it within a single thread block, using shared memory to store the heap.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Although this is a better algorithm, implementing it naively in CUDA still leaves per formance on the table. In the following kernel, we use the threads of a block to load the initial K elements into a shared memory heap in parallel, but then a single thread (thread 0) does all the work of iterating through the remaining elements and manag ing the heap. You can find this implementation in book.cu/4_optim/topK/kernels/1_ heap.cu.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Instead of having a single thread manage a data structure, we can parallelize the search for the maximum element at each step of the selection sort. This approach is imple mented in book.cu/4_optim/topK/kernels/2_warp.cu.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The algorithm is a parallel version of the naive selection sort. In each of the K iter ations, all threads in the block cooperate to find the single largest value among the currently unselected elements. This uses the same hierarchical block-level reduction pattern we’ve used before, but this time, the reduction needs to find both the max value and the index of that value.

regions.text: Top-k presents unique challenges compared to the other kernels we’ve optimized. Unlike GEMV, softmax, and LayerNorm where we perform the same operation on every element, top-k requires selective processing based on element values.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The naive selection sort achieves O(K × N) complexity with no parallelism and

regions.label: text
regions.text: The naive selection sort achieves O(K × N) complexity with no parallelism and executes entirely sequentially. The min-heap improves algorithmic complexity to O(N × log(K)) but remains single threaded, using only one thread to manage the heap structure. The parallel version parallelizes the search at each iteration using block-wide reductions but still requires K sequential iterations.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The sequential dependency in finding “the next maximum” after marking previous selections creates a fundamental bottleneck that limits how much parallel hardware can improve performance. The K outer iterations cannot be parallelized because each iteration depends on the results of all previous iterations.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Production top-k implementations often use radix sort or other fully parallel algo rithms when K is large, or bitonic sort networks, which can find all K elements simulta

regions.label: text
regions.text: Production top-k implementations often use radix sort or other fully parallel algo rithms when K is large, or bitonic sort networks, which can find all K elements simulta neously without sequential dependencies. For the small K values typical in MoE models ( K = 2 to K = 8 experts), the parallel reduction approach we’ve shown provides reason able performance.

regions.label: text
regions.text: We’ve arrived at the final and most computationally intensive kernel of the chapter: GEMM, or general matrix-matrix multiplication. GEMM is the workhorse of deep learning, forming the backbone of linear layers, convolutions, and many other oper ations. For transformers, it’s used to process entire batches of token embeddings simultaneously. Although GEMV is crucial for single-token generation, GEMM is what gives transformers their high throughput when processing prompts or training in batches.

regions.text: The precision loss is acceptable for most deep learning workloads. Weights and acti vations in transformer inference are routinely stored in FP16 or BF16 with little accu racy loss for most workloads (the two formats are not interchangeable: BF16 trades mantissa bits for exponent range). Training typically uses mixed precision: FP16 for forward and backward passes, and FP32 for the master weight copy and gradient accumulation. In the following code, the fp16 type is a typedef for CUDA’s __half type.

regions.text: GEMM: A compute-bound operation Unlike GEMV, softmax, and LayerNorm (which are memory-bound), GEMM is funda mentally compute-bound. This dramatically changes our optimization strategy. Con sider the following computational intensity analysis.

regions.label: text
regions.text: When multiplying an M × K matrix by a K × N matrix in FP16, we need to read MK + KN elements and write MN elements. The computation involves 2MNK FLOPs: MN dot products of length K . This gives an arithmetic intensity of 2MNK / [2(MK + KN + MN)] FLOPs per byte. For a concrete example, consider multiplying two 4096 × 4096 matrices. This requires approximately 67 MB of reads and 34 MB of writes, ³ totaling 101 MB of minimum memory traffic. The computation performs 2 × 4,096 operations, or roughly 137 billion FLOPs, yielding an arithmetic intensity of approxi mately 1,365 FLOPs per byte. Compare this with GEMV’s approximately 0.5 FLOPs per byte. The massive data reuse in GEMM (each matrix element participates in thou sands of multiplications) means we can amortize memory access costs across many computations.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The optimization goal for GEMM is to maximize compute utilization (target 80% to 90% of peak TFLOPS), not just memory bandwidth. We achieve this through coalesced memory access as a baseline requirement, followed by shared memory tiling to enable data reuse, register blocking to maximize arithmetic intensity, and finally, vec torization to saturate memory bandwidth when needed.

regions.label: text
regions.text: This kernel is a good starting point, but it suffers from the same memory access prob lems we’ve seen before, only magnified. A warp’s 32 threads have consecutive x and the same y . Their reads of A are K elements apart, so they are uncoalesced, and they all read the same element of B .

regions.label: text
regions.text: Profiling the naive GEMM kernel with NCU shows abysmal memory throughput despite the kernel being compute-bound in theory. The problem is memory access pat terns: each thread reads elements from a different row of A and a different column of B , creating completely uncoalesced accesses. The memory subsystem is bottlenecked by scattered requests instead of serving efficient burst transfers.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Data resuse analysis: Without tiling in the naive approach, each thread reads K elements from A and K elements from B , resulting in approximately 2,048 K global memory reads per block of 1024 threads. With tiling using BM = BN = 128 and BK = 8, each tile iteration has the block load BM*BK + BK*BN = 128*8 + 8*128 = 2,048 elements. These 2,048 elements are then reused for BM*BN = 16,384 dot product contributions, giving us a reuse factor of 16,384 / 2,048 = 8x per loaded element. This 8x reuse per tile, across K/8 tile iterations, dramatically reduces global memory pressure.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Why shared memory? Shared memory has roughly 19x higher aggregate bandwidth than global memory on the RTX 3090 (~18 TB/s across all SMs vs. 936 GB/s) and more than 10x lower latency (~30 cycles vs. hundreds). By loading tiles once and reusing them many times from shared memory, we shift from memory-bound to compute-bound.

regions.text: Currently we have 1,024 threads, each computing 1 output per thread, yielding 1,024 outputs per block. To maximize compute, we can use 1D blocktiling where each thread computes 8 outputs in a column, giving 8× more FMAs per load. This progression increases arithmetic intensity, allowing us to approach compute- bound performance.

regions.text: Each regM[i] value is multiplied by TN = 8 different regN[j] values (a whole row of the grid), and each regN[j] value is multiplied by TM = 8 different regM[i] values (a whole column). In total, TM + TN=16 loads enable TM × TN = 64 FMAs.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Arithmetic intensity: With 2D blocktiling where TM = TN = 8, we perform 16 loads per dotIdx iteration (8 from A , 8 from B ) to execute 64 FMAs, giving a ratio of 4 FMAs per load: 8× better than basic tiling!

regions.label: text
regions.text: Memory access analysis per thread: Per output tile of C across all K/BK iterations, we have approximately 2 * (K/BK) * (BM*BK + BK*BN) / numThreads ≈ K/(32*threads) GMEM loads per output. For SMEM loads, we have (K/BK) * (TM + TN) * BK = K * (TM + TN) per thread in total. The thread performs K * TM * TN FMAs in total, giving an arithmetic inten sity (FMAs per SMEM load) of KxTMxTN / (Kx(TM+TN)) = TMxTN/(TM+TN) = 4.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Performance effect is the following: The 2D blocktiling achieves compute through put of approximately 25.1 TFLOPS (70% of peak), delivering a 2.7× speedup over 1D tiling and roughly 84× over naive. The GPU now spends most of its time computing rather than waiting for memory, with the instruction mix showing roughly 60% FMA operations (compared to less than 10% in the naive kernel). The 2D blocktiling rep resents the inflection point where GEMM becomes truly compute-bound.

Four FP32 val ues fit in a 16-byte float4 or int4 ; eight FP8 values fit in an 8-byte int2 , and 16 FP8 val ues fit in a 16-byte int4 . Production kernels use the same pattern. For example, vLLM uses uint2 to carry four 16-bit lanes, while PyTorch kernels define alignment predicates before issuing wide loads..

regions.label: text
regions.text: hy vectorization still matters for compute - bound kernels W Even though we’re compute-bound, vectorized global memory access still helps. Each aligned int2 load moves four FP16 values (8 bytes) with one instruction instead of four scalar loads, reducing instruction count and freeing issue slots for FMAs. The align ment check ensures the vector path is used only when both source and destination are 8-byte aligned; otherwise, the scalar fallback preserves correctness.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Performance effect is the following: Vectorization pushes compute throughput to approximately 27.8 TFLOPS (78% of peak), yielding a 1.1× speedup over 2D tiling and roughly 93× over naive. Against the RTX 3090’s CUDA-core FP16 peak of about 35.6 TFLOPS, that leaves roughly 20% on the table. cuBLAS still reaches 66 TFLOPS on the same problem, but only by using tensor cores, the hardware chapter 7 introduces.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Several factors prevent us from reaching peak performance. Register pressure limits occupancy, and some shared memory bank conflicts remain. cuBLAS uses tensor cores (about 2× the FP32 CUDA-core rate on the RTX 3090, roughly 15× on an A100 or H100) has autotuned parameters for each matrix size, and implements double buffer ing with software pipelining.

regions.text: Regarding performance progression ( M = N = K = 4096 , FP16, RTX 3090), the naive implementation achieves around 0.3 TFLOPS with uncoalesced access and no data reuse. Coalescing pushes us to roughly 2.5 TFLOPS. Shared memory tiling adds basic reuse, reaching 3 TFLOPS. 1D blocktiling increases compute per thread by 8× and lands at 9.3 TFLOPS. 2D blocktiling delivers 64× compute per thread and marks the transition to compute-bound performance at 25 TFLOPS, about 70% of the card’s FP16 CUDA-core peak. Vectorization pushes to about 27 TFLOPS (77%). cuBLAS reaches 66 TFLOPS by using tensor cores, the hardware the chapter 7 material targets.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The progression falls into three phases: fixing memory access, staging data in shared memory, and raising the work each thread does. Phase one is dominated by memory bottlenecks; remapping threads for coalescing brings the first ~8× speedup but leaves the kernel bandwidth-limited. Phase two introduces shared memory tiles so each load serves multiple FMAs, yet the math units still idle between transactions. Phase three adopts block tiling so every thread computes a TM × TN tile in registers, lifting arithme tic intensity high enough to keep the SMs busy.

Phase one is dominated by memory bottlenecks; remapping threads for coalescing brings the first ~8× speedup but leaves the kernel bandwidth-limited. Phase two introduces shared memory tiles so each load serves multiple FMAs, yet the math units still idle between transactions. Phase three adopts block tiling so every thread computes a TM × TN tile in registers, lifting arithme tic intensity high enough to keep the SMs busy. Moving from a TM × 1 tile to TM × TN gives every element of A and B many more reuse opportunities. Each B load feeds TM outputs, each A load feeds TN outputs, so TM + TN loads feed TM × TN FMAs (16 loads and 64 FMAs at TM = TN = 8).

regions.text: Tensor cores are specialized hardware units within each streaming multiproces sor (SM) that execute matrix multiply-accumulate operations at significantly higher throughput than CUDA cores. Tensor cores use mixed precision: they multiply at low precision (FP16 or BF16) but accumulate at higher precision (FP32), combining high throughput with numerical stability. regions.label: text
regions.text: A CUDA core performs one fused multiply- add (two FLOPs) per clock cycle. A tensor core, by contrast, performs an entire 16 ×16 × 16 or larger matrix operation in a single instruction. Because the accumulator runs at FP32 while the inputs are FP16, training remains numerically stable despite the lower- precision multiplications: rounding errors don’t drift and compound across thousands of gradient steps. On an H100, this translates to dramatic performance differences: 67 TFLOPS for FP32 on CUDA cores versus 989.5 TFLOPS for dense FP16 on tensor cores, roughly a 15× improvement. (NVIDIA’s head line figure of 1,979 TFLOPS additionally assumes 2:4 structured sparsity, which doubles the number but no longer compares like for like.)

regions.text: Figure 7.1 shows the full cuBLAS-style GEMM: C = alpha * (A @ B) + beta * C , with scalar scaling and accumulation into an existing matrix. Both cuBLAS and tensor cores support various precision formats (FP16, BF16, TensorFloat-32 [TF32, which we enabled back in chapter 4], FP8, and FP4 on newer architectures), with the accumula tor typically at FP32 regardless of input type. Tensor core Matrix Multiply- Accumulate (MMA) instructions strip this down to D = A * B + C , where C is simply the accumulator from the previous iteration, with no scalar weighting. The alpha/beta scaling that cuBLAS provides is handled as a separate epilogue step, not by the tensor core hard ware itself.

We will spend most of this chapter on WGMMA. ¡ TCGen05 (Blackwell, 2024) —The fifth-generation tensor core instruction on the B200 further improves efficiency and adds support for FP4 precision. B200 GPUs are now available on major cloud providers, and CUTLASS has supported TCGen05 since version 3.8, and the 4.x line extends that support across the Blackwell family. We discuss TCGen05 conceptually in this chapter’s conclusion but defer implementation to chapter 11 (CUTLASS), where library abstractions make it more accessible.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Note that dropping precision roughly doubles throughput at each step (TF32 to FP16 to FP8 to FP4). Hopper delivers about a 3× jump over Ampere at the same pre cision, and Blackwell’s dual-die B200 roughly doubles Hopper again. Consumer RTX boards expose many of the same tensor-core instructions but at lower throughput due to fewer SMs and tighter power envelopes. For example, the RTX 3090’s tensor core TF32 throughput equals its CUDA core FP32 throughput (35.6 TFLOPS), while the data center A100 delivers over 4× that (156 TFLOPS) at the same precision. This cre ates an accessibility ladder: most readers can practice on RTX cards today, while A100, H100, and B200 illustrate where the hardware is heading.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The basic WMMA workflow mirrors the tiling patterns from chapter 6. Each thread block claims a tile of the output matrix, stages the matching input tiles in shared mem ory, and lets its warps pull fragments with load_matrix_sync . Those fragments feed mma_sync , the results land back in shared memory via store_matrix_sync , and the block finally writes the accumulated tile to global memory.

regions.text: To understand WMMA’s tiling hierarchy, picture a large grid representing the output matrix, as shown in figure 7.2. The thread block claims a 128 × 128 region of that grid.

regions.label: text
regions.text: To understand WMMA’s tiling hierarchy, picture a large grid representing the output matrix, as shown in figure 7.2. The thread block claims a 128 × 128 region of that grid. Within that region, we assign each warp a smaller rectangle (32 × 64 in our case). Each warp then tiles its rectangle with 16 × 16 WMMA operations, stepping through it systematically. This hierarchy maps naturally to the GPU’s execution model: warps execute independently, but all threads within a warp operate in lockstep.

regions.text: WMMA distributes each 16 × 16 tile across all 32 threads of a warp through “frag ments.” A fragment is one thread’s share of the 16 × 16 tile, held in its registers. load_ matrix_sync fills every thread’s fragment, and the threads never need to know which elements they hold. When you call mma_sync , all 32 threads simultaneously feed their fragment data to the tensor core, which computes the full 16 × 16 × 16 operation in hardware. This is fundamentally different from chapter 6, where each thread explicitly managed every value it computed.

regions.title: 7.2.2 Loading data with WMMA
regions.text: 7.2.2 Loading data with WMMA

regions.label: text
regions.text: 7.2.2 Loading data with WMMA

regions.label: text
regions.text: Before the warp can use WMMA operations, we need to load tiles from global memory into shared memory. This stage is still manual: WMMA automates the matrix multiply, not the memory movement.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The key challenge is distributing work across 256 threads (our block size) to load a 128 × 16 tile of A and a 16 × 128 tile of B . Each thread should load eight FP16 values (one int4 vector) to maximize memory bandwidth. The arithmetic for computing each thread’s load position is designed around this constraint.

regions.label: text
regions.text: For matrix A (128 rows × 16 columns), we want adjacent threads to load adjacent columns for coalescing. If each thread loads eight columns, we need two threads per

regions.label: text
regions.text: For matrix A (128 rows × 16 columns), we want adjacent threads to load adjacent columns for coalescing. If each thread loads eight columns, we need two threads per row (16 / 8 = 2). This is why tid / 2 gives us the row index—every two threads advance to the next row. The column offset (tid % 2) * 8 alternates between 0 and 8, giving the two threads in each row their nonoverlapping eight-element chunks.

regions.label: text
regions.text: For matrix B (16 rows × 128 columns), we need 16 threads per row (128 / 8 = 16). Thus, tid / 16 gives us the row index (every 16 threads start a new row), and (tid % 16) * 8 gives each thread its column offset within that row. The following listing shows this vectorized loading pattern.

regions.label: text
regions.text: When we call load_matrix_sync , something interesting happens under the hood. The hardware examines the shared memory pointer and the leading dimension, then automatically gives each of the 32 threads its assigned portion of the 16 × 16 tile to hold in registers. Thread 0 doesn’t get elements [0–7], and thread 1 doesn’t get elements [8–15]; the distribution is more sophisticated, optimized for the tensor core’s internal data flow. We don’t need to know the distribution pattern. We declare the fragment, call the load function, and trust the hardware to handle the rest. The following listing demonstrates this fragment loading.

regions.label: text
regions.text: You might notice that the 128 × 128 block tile divides into only eight warp regions (four along M, two along N), which means eight warps per block, or 256 threads. A block can hold up to 32 warps (1,024 threads), but fewer warps give each warp more work. Each of our eight warps handles a 2 × 4 grid of 16 × 16 WMMA operations, per forming eight tensor core instructions per K-tile iteration. If we split the same 128 × 128 block across 32 warps, each warp would handle just a 2 × 1 grid: only two tensor core instructions per iteration. The fragment load overhead (loading A and B fragments from shared memory) would dominate the actual compute. Eight warps is the sweet spot where each warp does enough work to amortize that overhead while still staying within SM register and shared memory limits.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The mma_sync operation is where hardware acceleration happens. This single function call triggers the tensor core to perform 16 × 16 × 16 = 4,096 multiply-accumulate oper ations. All 32 threads in the warp participate, but the hardware manages the details of how the work is distributed. Note a critical detail in the fragment types: inputs A and B use half (FP16) for throughput, but the accumulator fragment uses float (FP32) to prevent rounding errors from accumulating across iterations. This mixed-precision design is what makes tensor cores practical for training: without the higher-precision accumulator, gradient updates would drift, and training would become unstable.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Instead of operating at warp granularity (32 threads), WGMMA operates on warp groups (128 threads = 4 warps). Instead of using synchronous operations that block until complete, WGMMA uses asynchronous instructions that issue operations and return immediately. And instead of manually loading data from global to shared memory, WGMMA integrates with the Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA), a dedicated direct mem ory access (DMA) engine that handles data movement independently of the threads. Let’s unpack why each of these changes exists.

regions.label: paragraph_title
regions.title: Instead of operating at warp granularity (32 threads), WGMMA operates on warp groups (128 threads = 4 warps). Instead of using synchronous operations that block until complete, WGMMA uses asynchronous instructions that issue operations and return immediately. And instead of manually loading data from global to shared memory, WGMMA integrates with the Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA), a dedicated direct mem ory access (DMA) engine that handles data movement independently of the threads. Let’s unpack why each of these changes exists.

regions.text: Why four warps? Each Hopper SM contains four warp schedulers, each capable of issuing instructions to one warp per cycle. A warp group aligns exactly with this hard ware: all four schedulers issue the same WGMMA instruction on the same cycle, feed ing 128 threads’ worth of register data to the tensor core in a single coordinated step. Blocks do not execute in lockstep (their warps can be at different program counters), so a block is too loose a grouping. Individual warps are too narrow to saturate the wider tensor core units on Hopper.

regions.label: text
regions.text: four warps execute together as a warp group, all reaching the WGMMA instruction at the same time. This is stricter than normal thread cooperation: these 128 threads must be at the same program counter when the instruction fires. WGMMA operates on 64 × 64 tiles instead of 16 × 16 tiles. A single m64n64k16 instruc tion performs 65,536 FMAs, and four of them complete a full 64 × 64 × 64 tile: 262,144 FMAs in total. The tensor core needs data from all 128 threads simultaneously to fill its wider execution units. That’s 4× the threads, 16× the tile area, and 16× the FMAs per instruction: 4× the work per thread. Figure 7.4 shows this tiling hierarchy.

The %ctaid.x , %ntid.x , and %tid.x registers are built-in PTX registers for blockIdx.x , blockDim.x , and threadIdx.x . The mad.lo.s32 instruction is a fused multiply-add on integers, exactly our blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x index cal culation. regions.label: text
regions.text: The next optimization is straightforward: increase tile sizes. Larger tiles improve arithmetic intensity (compute-to-memory ratio) and reduce the overhead of loading tiles. Think of it this way: every time we load a tile from global memory, we pay a fixed latency cost. With a 64 × 64 tile, we perform 262,144 operations (64 × 64 × 64 with K = 64) per load. With a 128 × 128 tile, we perform 1,048,576 operations per load, four times the computation for twice the bytes loaded. Table 7.2 shows the comparison.

regions.title: The next optimization is straightforward: increase tile sizes. Larger tiles improve arithmetic intensity (compute-to-memory ratio) and reduce the overhead of loading tiles. Think of it this way: every time we load a tile from global memory, we pay a fixed latency cost. With a 64 × 64 tile, we perform 262,144 operations (64 × 64 × 64 with K = 64) per load. With a 128 × 128 tile, we perform 1,048,576 operations per load, four times the computation for twice the bytes loaded. Table 7.2 shows the comparison.

regions.label: text
regions.text: But we are still loading tiles synchronously, blocking the warp group until data arrives from global memory. This leaves the tensor cores idle during loads. The next optimiza tion addresses this.

regions.label: paragraph_title
regions.title: 7.3.4 WGMMA with asynchronous memory operations
regions.text: 7.3.4 WGMMA with asynchronous memory operations

regions.label: text
regions.text: 7.3.4 WGMMA with asynchronous memory operations

regions.label: text
regions.text: The TMA is Hopper’s dedicated DMA engine for tensor data movement. TMA allows threads to issue a load operation and immediately return to computation while the hardware manages the data transfer in the background.

regions.label: text
regions.text: In chapter 6’s tiled GEMM, every thread loaded its share of a tile, waited at __syncthreads() , and then computed, so loading and math took turns. Our WGMMA kernels so far copy tiles with TMA, but every thread still waits for each copy before com puting. The fix is the one PyTorch’s DataLoader uses, where worker processes prepare the next batch while the GPU trains on the current one. In K11, a producer thread asks TMA for upcoming tiles while the consumer threads run WGMMA on tiles that have already arrived.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Here’s how the pattern looks in code: a tiny producer set (often just thread 0) issues the TMA copies that move data from global to shared memory, the remaining threads consume that data via WGMMA, and CUDA barriers keep both sides in lockstep so the tensor cores never read half-delivered tiles. The following listing demonstrates the producer- consumer coordination.

Thread 0 (the pro ducer) calls the TMA load function, which dispatches the request to the hardware DMA engine and returns immediately; thread 0 doesn’t wait for the transfer to com plete. Instead, it “arrives” at a barrier, announcing that it has initiated a transaction. All other threads (consumers) also arrive at the barrier, but with no transaction. The bar rier tracks: “I’m expecting 128 arrivals (one per thread) and 1 transaction (the TMA load).”

regions.text: In the code, this pattern manifests as multiple regions in shared memory, each with its own barrier. The producer issues TMA loads to all three regions, staggered across

regions.label: text
regions.text: In the code, this pattern manifests as multiple regions in shared memory, each with its own barrier. The producer issues TMA loads to all three regions, staggered across loop iterations. Consumers process whichever region has completed its load. The bar riers ensure correctness: no consumer touches a region until its TMA load finishes, and no producer overwrites a region until consumers are done with it. K11 already ran this pipeline with five buffers and one consumer warp group. The jump from 504 to 618 TFLOPS comes from the second consumer warp group and the wider 128 × 256 tile.

regions.text: Figure 7.5 visualizes this producer-consumer pipeline. The producer warp group (WG0) issues TMA loads into a rotating set of three shared memory buffers. After the initial fill, all three warp groups are active at every time step: the producer always loads while both consumers compute, and barriers ensure that no warp group touches a buffer that isn’t ready.

regions.label: text
regions.text: CUDA core phase (K1–K6) —Manual optimizations achieved an 86× speedup through memory hierarchy optimization. The largest jump came from memory coalescing (11×), which fixed how threads access global memory. Shared mem ory added another 2×, register tiling squeezed out 3.3×, and vectorization gave a final 1.2×. Each optimization attacked a different bottleneck: first memory band width, then reuse, then arithmetic intensity, and then transaction efficiency.

regions.text: CUDA core phase (K1–K6) —Manual optimizations achieved an 86× speedup through memory hierarchy optimization. The largest jump came from memory coalescing (11×), which fixed how threads access global memory. Shared mem ory added another 2×, register tiling squeezed out 3.3×, and vectorization gave a final 1.2×. Each optimization attacked a different bottleneck: first memory band width, then reuse, then arithmetic intensity, and then transaction efficiency. The WMMA jump (K6 → K8) —Moving from manual CUDA cores (43 TFLOPS) to WMMA (71 TFLOPS) gave us a 1.7× speedup. The algorithm is the same, but with fixed-function units performing the multiply-accumulate instead of general- purpose ALUs. The 1.7× speedup may seem modest compared with market ing claims of “10 to 20× speedups,” but that’s because our chapter 6 kernel was already highly optimized. Against a naive implementation, WMMA shows a 142× speedup.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The WGMMA jump (K8 → K9) —The leap from WMMA (71 TFLOPS) to basic WGMMA (318 TFLOPS) is where we see a 4.5× improvement. This comes from two sources: larger tiles (64 × 64 instead of 16 × 16) mean more work per instruc tion, and warp group execution (128 threads instead of 32) provides better occupancy and latency hiding. The hardware can keep more tensor cores busy simultaneously.

CUTLASS provides high-level abstractions over WMMA and WGMMA, handles edge cases, and includes highly optimized templates for com mon patterns. Hand-tuned kernels are specialized. Change the architecture, the SM count, or the matrix shapes, and a kernel can lose much of its speed. Our K12 kernel does not run on Blackwell at all, because wgmma requires sm_90a (section 7.7). Before putting weeks into a kernel, consider where else it will run.

regions.label: text
regions.text: In chapter 6, we discovered that keeping partial results in registers was the key to high performance. Each thread maintained a small 2D array of accumulator values

regions.label: text
regions.text: In chapter 6, we discovered that keeping partial results in registers was the key to high performance. Each thread maintained a small 2D array of accumulator values (TM × TN), loaded small vectors from shared memory into temporary registers, computed outer products, and accumulated the results. This register tiling pattern emerged from first principles: registers are the fastest memory, so we maximize the work done per register load.

regions.label: text
regions.text: In chapter 6, we spent considerable effort on vectorized memory transfers. We care fully cast pointers to float4 types, checked alignment, handled edge cases when matrix dimensions weren’t divisible by 4, and manually unrolled loops to ensure the compiler generated wide load instructions. This was tedious but necessary: wide loads maximize memory bandwidth by moving 128 bits at a time instead of 32 bits.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The single TMA call replaces all the manual vectorization logic. The descriptor we created earlier already encodes the tensor shape, strides, alignment requirements, and swizzling patterns, so cp_async_bulk_tensor_2d_global_to_shared computes the addresses, issues the widest possible memory transactions, applies the swizzle that avoids bank conflicts, overlaps the transfer with ongoing compute, and trips the barrier once the data arrives.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Despite the automation, several critical optimizations remain the programmer’s responsibility. You must still choose grid dimensions, block dimensions, and tile sizes for kernel launches, as these decisions dramatically affect occupancy and perfor mance. Tensor cores handle individual tiles, but you decide how to partition the full matrix across blocks and how to iterate across the K dimension. For WGMMA, you must manage memory layout: the instruction reads operands from shared memory in either K -major or MN -major layout, selected per operand by descriptor immediates, and the declared layout must match how you staged the data. Our kernels stage col umn-major tiles; converting a 4096 × 4096 matrix host-side can cost around 30 ms, more than the GEMM itself, so you choose whether to preconvert, store matrices natively in the matching layout, or stage the layout change during the shared-mem ory load.

regions.text: The WGMMA instruction includes the shared memory read, multiply-accumulate, and register update in a single instruction. The intermediate step (loading from shared to registers) has disappeared from the programmer’s view. The hardware still performs this transfer, but it’s fused into the WGMMA instruction itself. This reduces instruction count, register pressure, and synchronization overhead. TCGen05 also moves the accumulator out of registers. A single thread issues tcgen05. mma, and the result accumulates in tensor memory (TMEM), a dedicated on-chip memory, instead of in the registers of a 128-thread warp group.

regions.label: footer
regions.text: 7.6.4 What you still optimize manually Despite the automation, several critical optimizations remain the programmer’s responsibility. You must still choose grid dimensions, block dimensions, and tile sizes for kernel launches, as these decisions dramatically affect occupancy and perfor mance. Tensor cores handle individual tiles, but you decide how to partition the full matrix across blocks and how to iterate across the K dimension. For WGMMA, you must manage memory layout: the instruction reads operands from shared memory in either K -major or MN -major layout, selected per operand by descriptor immediates, and the declared layout must match how you staged the data. Our kernels stage col umn-major tiles; converting a 4096 × 4096 matrix host-side can cost around 30 ms, more than the GEMM itself, so you choose whether to preconvert, store matrices natively in the matching layout, or stage the layout change during the shared-mem ory load. With TMA and producer-consumer patterns, you design the pipeline architecture: decide how many producer threads to use, how many stages to include in the cir cular buffer, and which barriers coordinate producers and consumers. For epilogue operations beyond basic matrix multiplication, such as adding bias terms or apply ing activation functions, you implement these separately, though libraries like CUT LASS provide abstractions for common patterns. Finally, although wgmma.mma_async is asynchronous, you still place warpgroup_arrive() , warpgroup_commit_batch() , and warpgroup_wait<N>() instructions manually. Incorrect synchronization causes race conditions or deadlocks, so understanding the async programming model remains essential.

regions.text: 7.7 TCGen05: Blackwell’s tensor cores Before we conclude, let’s briefly examine TCGen05, the fifth-generation tensor core instruction set introduced with NVIDIA’s Blackwell architecture (B200). Although we won’t implement TCGen05 kernels in this chapter, understanding its capabilities pro vides context for where tensor core programming is headed. B200 GPUs are broadly available as of early 2026: the major cloud providers (AWS P6-B200 instances, Google Cloud A4 VMs, Azure ND B200 v6) all offer Blackwell access, along with GPU-focused providers like CoreWeave, Lambda Labs, RunPod, and Modal. CUTLASS 4.2+ includes comprehensive TCGen05 examples.

With TMA and producer-consumer patterns, you design the pipeline architecture: decide how many producer threads to use, how many stages to include in the cir cular buffer, and which barriers coordinate producers and consumers. For epilogue operations beyond basic matrix multiplication, such as adding bias terms or apply ing activation functions, you implement these separately, though libraries like CUT LASS provide abstractions for common patterns. Finally, although wgmma.mma_async is asynchronous, you still place warpgroup_arrive() , warpgroup_commit_batch() , and warpgroup_wait<N>() instructions manually. Incorrect synchronization causes race conditions or deadlocks, so understanding the async programming model remains essential.

regions.text: The WGMMA instruction includes the shared memory read, multiply-accumulate, and register update in a single instruction. The intermediate step (loading from shared to registers) has disappeared from the programmer’s view. The hardware still performs this transfer, but it’s fused into the WGMMA instruction itself. This reduces instruction count, register pressure, and synchronization overhead. TCGen05 also moves the accumulator out of registers. A single thread issues tcgen05. mma, and the result accumulates in tensor memory (TMEM), a dedicated on-chip memory, instead of in the registers of a 128-thread warp group.

B200 GPUs are broadly available as of early 2026: the major cloud providers (AWS P6-B200 instances, Google Cloud A4 VMs, Azure ND B200 v6) all offer Blackwell access, along with GPU-focused providers like CoreWeave, Lambda Labs, RunPod, and Modal. CUTLASS 4.2+ includes comprehensive TCGen05 examples.

regions.text: In the last chapter, we explored tensor cores and took GEMM from 43 to 618 TFLOPS on an H100. Our focus was almost entirely on optimizing raw arithmetic, ensuring that every GPU cycle was spent doing useful math. But as we move into optimizing complex operations like the attention mechanism, we encounter a different kind of performance barrier.

This chapter introduces Flash Attention, a technique that redesigns the attention algorithm to eliminate this HBM bottleneck. The algorithm violates several intuitions that experienced GPU programmers have built up from working with simpler opera tions. These are the most common misconceptions: that tiling attention should work the same way as tiling GEMM, that partial softmax across tiles requires global communi cation between thread blocks, and that the familiar “inching inwards” loop from matrix multiplication has no place in the algorithm.

regions.text: To understand why Flash Attention is necessary, we must first analyze the standard imple mentation of the attention mechanism. The core of attention is a sequence of three operations. First, we calculate the dot product of the query ( Q ) and key ( K ) matrices to produce a score matrix S with S = Q @ K.T . Next, we apply a softmax function to the score matrix S to get the attention weights P , computing P = softmax(S) . Finally, we multiply the attention weights P by the value ( V ) matrix to get the final output O with O = P @ V .

regions.text: Let’s consider the shapes of these matrices for a typical language model. If we have a sequence of length N and a head dimension d , then Q , K , and V each have shape (N, d) . The intermediate matrix S (and P ) will have shape (N, N) . For a context length N of 8,192, this S matrix would be 8192 × 8192. If we use 32-bit floats, this single matrix requires 8192 * 8192 * 4 bytes, which is 268 megabytes. For a modern model with a 128K context length, this grows to over 65 gigabytes for a single attention head.

regions.text: Before we examine the Flash Attention solution, we need to confront a fundamental tension. If you already understand how tiled matrix multiplication works on GPUs, you might be thinking, “This seems straightforward. Just break the computation into tiles that fit in SRAM, as we do for GEMM.” But attention has a property that makes it funda mentally different from matrix multiplication, and this difference is the source of the most common misconceptions about Flash Attention.

regions.text: The core idea behind tiling is to break down the large Q , K , and V matrices into smaller blocks. We compute the sum of exponen tials sum(exp(score - m)) and store it as l . When we process the second tile, with scores for columns 128 through 255, we might find a new, larger maximum value. Let’s call this new local maximum m_new . This new maximum might be larger than our running maximum m .

regions.text: need to “rescale” our previous running sum to be consistent with the new maximum m_ new . The correction factor is exp(m_old - m_new) . We multiply our running sum l by this correction factor, then add the new partial sum computed with the new maximum. This ensures that when we finally divide by l at the end, we get exactly the same result as if we had computed the softmax over the entire row at once. In floating point, it matches this up to the usual rounding differences that come from reordering additions. What it never does is materialize the full row of scores in memory.

Read it from left to right: the dashed strip at the top is the full row of scores that never exists in memory, and each step below it pulls one 128-column tile into SRAM and folds it into the three running values m , l , and O . The arrows between steps carry the correction factor exp(m_old - m_new) , which rescales the old state whenever a new tile raises the maxi mum. After the last tile, dividing O by l yields exactly the result a full-row softmax would have produced.

It uses three separate kernel launches, which we will examine one by one.

regions.text: 8.3.2 Understanding the work distribution strategy Before we look at the fused Flash Attention kernel, we need to address the second major misconception: Where do the running statistics live? If we compute softmax iter atively across tiles while GPUs parallelize work across many thread blocks, you might reasonably conclude that different thread blocks must be working on different tiles of the same output row. To share the running maximum m and running sum l , those sta tistics would need to live in global HBM, where all thread blocks can access them. This would destroy the performance gains we’re trying to achieve.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The flaw is in the assumption about how work is distributed. In a standard tiled GEMM, we parallelize across both output dimensions. If we’re computing a matrix C with shape (M, N) , we might launch a grid of thread blocks, with each thread block computing a tile of the output. Block (0,0) computes C[0:32, 0:32] , block (0,1) computes C[0:32, 32:64] , and so on. All these blocks work independently and simultaneously.

regions.text: 8.3.3 The three-level loop hierarchy Now we need to address the third major misconception—one that often troubles programmers who have a deep understanding of tiled GEMM. If you’ve built a high-performance matrix multiplication kernel, you know that computing an out put tile requires inching inward over the shared inner dimension. To compute C[i,j] = A[i,:] @ B[:,j] , you load a slice of A and a slice of B , multiply them, load the next slices, multiply, and accumulate until you’ve traversed the full inner dimension. So when you learn that Flash Attention has a “sequential loop across the sequence length,” you might try to reconcile this with your GEMM intuition and become deeply confused. How can we compute a full tile of scores without looping over the head dimension d ? Where does the inching inward pattern fit into the “horizontal march” across the sequence? Figure 8.5 shows this three-level nesting. The answer is that Flash Attention has a three-level loop hierarchy, and your GEMM intuition is not wrong. It’s just operating at a different level. At the grid level, we have parallelism across different output row tiles. Different thread blocks compute different bricks of output rows independently. At the thread block level, we have the sequential horizontal march across the sequence length. This is the main Flash Attention loop, where we iterate through tiles of K and V . At the warp and thread level, we have the inching inwards loop over the head dimension d .

regions.label: number
regions.text: This is a standard mini-GEMM kernel that computes a tile of scores by accumulating partial products. These loops nest. The innermost inching inwards loop is completely contained within a single iteration of the middle horizontal march loop. When thread block 0 processes K and V tiles corresponding to sequence positions 0 to 127, it performs a com plete GEMM-style computation to produce a full tile of scores for those positions. This tile is consumed immediately by the online softmax update, and then the middle loop advances to the next K and V tiles for positions 128 to 255. The inner GEMM computa tion runs again, producing another complete tile of scores, which is again consumed immediately. The scores are never accumulated across iterations of the middle loop. Each iteration of the horizontal march produces a complete partial score tile, applies online softmax, updates the output accumulator, and then discards the scores before moving to the next iteration.

regions.label: number
regions.text: This nested structure explains why Flash Attention doesn’t violate your understanding of matrix multiplication. The matrix multiplications ( Q @ K.T and P @ V ) are performed using exactly the techniques you know, with inner loops accumulating over the shared dimension. Flash Attention adds an outer sequential loop around these GEMM opera tions and uses online softmax to combine the results in a way that maintains mathemat ical correctness without materializing the full attention matrix.

regions.label: number
regions.text: This is a standard mini-GEMM kernel that computes a tile of scores by accumulating partial products. These loops nest. The innermost inching inwards loop is completely contained within a single iteration of the middle horizontal march loop. When thread block 0 processes K and V tiles corresponding to sequence positions 0 to 127, it performs a com plete GEMM-style computation to produce a full tile of scores for those positions. This tile is consumed immediately by the online softmax update, and then the middle loop advances to the next K and V tiles for positions 128 to 255. The inner GEMM computa tion runs again, producing another complete tile of scores, which is again consumed immediately. The scores are never accumulated across iterations of the middle loop. Each iteration of the horizontal march produces a complete partial score tile, applies online softmax, updates the output accumulator, and then discards the scores before moving to the next iteration.

regions.text: implementation with a clear mental model. This single, monolithic kernel replaces the three separate kernels from the naive implementation. By keeping the entire computation on chip and processing the matrices in small tiles, we avoid the costly round trips to HBM. Our implementation uses WMMA tensor core instructions for the heavy lifting of matrix multiplication, which requires us to use half precision ( FP16 ) for the inputs.

regions.label: text
regions.text: As you read through the kernel code, keep in mind the four key insights we developed. First, we’re computing an exact, iterative softmax using correction fac tors, not approximate local softmaxes. Second, each thread block owns its output rows completely and maintains all state in private SRAM. Third, the familiar GEMM inching- inwards loop is nested inside the horizontal march loop. Fourth, the output accumulator is a single running total that gets updated in place, not a growing list of partials.

regions.text: When we compute Pij @ Vj for the first tile, we add it to Oi , which starts at zero. When we process the second tile and compute a new Pij @ Vj , we don’t store it sep arately. We scale the existing value in Oi by the correction factor (to account for the updated maximum), then add the new contribution, and overwrite the old value in Oi , as shown in listing 8.10. regions.text: need to be stored? The answer is no, and understanding why requires a shift in how you think about accumulation. The Oi buffer in SRAM is not one of many partial tiles. It is a single running total, like a bank account balance or a scratchpad where you update your exam score as you grade each question. When we compute Pij @ Vj for the first tile, we add it to Oi , which starts at zero. When we process the second tile and compute a new Pij @ Vj , we don’t store it sep arately. We scale the existing value in Oi by the correction factor (to account for the updated maximum), then add the new contribution, and overwrite the old value in Oi , as shown in listing 8.10. The information from the first tile is not lost. It has been absorbed into the updated total. No matter how many tiles we process, we always have exactly one Oi buffer in SRAM, and it always holds the sum of all corrected contribu tions seen so far.

regions.label: text
regions.text: These speedups deserve a careful caveat. Our comparison bundles three separate advantages into one number. First, the Flash Attention algorithm itself: tiling and online 2 softmax eliminate the O(N ) HBM round trips for the intermediate score matrix. Sec ond, the FA kernel uses FP16 tensor cores for matrix multiplication, while the naive kernel uses FP32 CUDA cores. Tensor cores are fundamentally faster at matrix math, so part of the speedup comes from the precision difference, not the algorithm. Third, the FA kernel launches once for all 128 heads via a 2D grid, while the naive kernel loops over heads on the host and launches 384 separate kernels (128 heads × 3 kernels each). Kernel launch overhead and serialization account for some of the gap, especially at shorter sequences where per-kernel compute is small.

We chose not to do that here because the whole point of Flash Atten tion is that it enables fusion: you can’t fuse three separate kernels that each need the full N × N matrix, but you can fuse tiled operations that need only small on-chip buf fers. The fusion advantage and the tensor core advantage are part of the story, not con founds to be eliminated.

regions.text: 8.4 The evolution of Flash Attention The Flash Attention kernel we built represents the foundational ideas behind this optimization technique. Since the original Flash Attention paper (Dao, Fu, Ermon, Rudra, and Ré, “FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness,” https: / /arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135 ), there have been three major iter ations, each bringing substantial performance improvements and new optimization techniques.

regions.text: 8.4.1 Flash Attention 1 and 2 The original Flash Attention established the core algorithmic foundation we explored in this chapter. The key innovation was recognizing that the memory bot tleneck, not computation, was the limiting factor for attention at long sequence lengths. By applying classical techniques from high-performance computing, til ing and recomputation, to the specific structure of the attention mechanism, the algorithm eliminated the need to materialize the massive N × N attention matri ces in HBM. Instead, it processed attention in blocks small enough to fit in SRAM, so the intermediate score and probability matrices never touch slow memory. This ² approach reduced memory usage from O(N ) to O(N) and achieved 2 to 4× speed ups over optimized baselines. Flash Attention 1 parallelized over batch size and the number of attention heads. Instead, it processed attention in blocks small enough to fit in SRAM, so the intermediate score and probability matrices never touch slow memory. This ² approach reduced memory usage from O(N ) to O(N) and achieved 2 to 4× speed ups over optimized baselines.

Data center GPUs have specialized tensor core units that make matrix multiplication roughly 15× faster than general arithmetic operations (H100: 989.5 dense FP16 tensor TFLOPS versus 67 FP32 TFLOPS; on con sumer parts the gap is closer to 2×). Every cycle spent on non-matmul work (computing exponentials, finding maximums, normalizing) is many cycles not spent on matmuls. Flash Attention 2 introduced deferred scaling and logsumexp storage to minimize these operations while maintaining correctness. regions.text: and the backward pass was even slower, at 25% to 35%. In contrast, optimized matrix multiplications routinely achieve 80% to 90% utilization. The bottleneck had shifted from memory bandwidth to suboptimal parallelism and work distribution. Flash Attention 2 (Tri Dao, “FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Paral lelism and Work Partitioning,” https: / /arxiv.org/abs/2307.08691 ) addressed the per formance gap through three focused improvements: algorithmic tweaks to reduce non-matmul operations, better parallelism across sequence lengths, and smarter work partitioning within thread blocks. The first change targets non-matmul work. Data center GPUs have specialized tensor core units that make matrix multiplication roughly 15× faster than general arithmetic operations (H100: 989.5 dense FP16 tensor TFLOPS versus 67 FP32 TFLOPS; on con sumer parts the gap is closer to 2×). Every cycle spent on non-matmul work (computing exponentials, finding maximums, normalizing) is many cycles not spent on matmuls. Flash Attention 2 introduced deferred scaling and logsumexp storage to minimize these operations while maintaining correctness. The parallelism and work partitioning improvements were more fundamental. Flash Attention 2 added parallelization over the sequence-length dimension. The outer loop over output blocks became embarrassingly parallel, with different thread blocks han dling different output tiles independently. This kept the GPU busy even when process ing single long sequences. The work partitioning changes targeted shared memory traffic. Flash Attention 1 split K and V across warps using a “split- K ” scheme. Each warp computed part of QK^T , wrote intermediate results to shared memory, synchronized, and then combined the results. This created unnecessary shared memory reads and writes. Flash Attention 2 instead split Q across warps while keeping K and V accessible to all warps. After computing its slice of QK^T , each warp independently multiplied it with V to get its output slice. No synchronization was needed. This reduced shared memory traffic and yielded a measurable speedup. Together, these improvements delivered roughly a 2× speedup over Flash Attention 1, reaching 50% to 73% of theoretical throughput on A100 GPUs. End-to-end training of GPT-style models achieved 225 TFLOPs/s per A100, a 1.3× improvement over Flash Attention 1 and 2.8× over the non-Flash baseline. Our implementation in this chapter captures the essential ideas from Flash Atten tion 1 and 2: tiling to fit data in SRAM, online softmax for numerically stable streaming computation, and kernel fusion to eliminate memory bottlenecks. As we saw in table 8.1, our WMMA-based kernel achieves up to approximately 15× speedup over the naive baseline. But production implementations push much further, reaching 75% of theo retical hardware throughput on modern GPUs.

regions.text: The fix was warp specialization. Producer warps stream data via TMA into circular buffers while consumer warps run WGMMA on completed tiles, coordinated by light weight barriers. regions.label: doc_title
regions.title: Flash Attention 4 targets Blackwell with two algorithmic changes and a more complex pipeline. First, software exponentials replace hardware SFUs (only 4 per SM vs. 128+ CUDA cores), using a cubic polynomial approximation via Horner’s method that matches SFU precision for BF16 while avoiding the bottleneck. Second, smarter resca ling skips the softmax correction when the running maximum changes by less than a stability threshold, reducing rescaling operations by 10×.

First, software exponentials replace hardware SFUs (only 4 per SM vs. 128+ CUDA cores), using a cubic polynomial approximation via Horner’s method that matches SFU precision for BF16 while avoiding the bottleneck. The pipeline expands from two warpgroups to five specialized warp types: Load, MMA, Softmax, Correction, and Epilogue warps, all running concurrently on persistent kernel blocks scheduled by a tile dispatcher. This delivers a reported 20% speedup over NVIDIA’s cuDNN attention kernels but at a significant cost in complexity: the kernel is highly architecture- specific and requires substantial rewriting for each GPU genera tion, pushing framework developers toward abstractions like CUTLASS and CuTe. (Our understanding of Flash Attention 4 is based on the reverse-engineering work by Frye, Wang, and Feng at Modal: https: / /modal.com/blog/reverse-engineer-flash-attention-4 . The Flash Attention imple mentations are open source: https: / /github.com/Dao-AILab/

The shift from mate rializing attention matrices to tiling and online softmax delivered the largest single speedup. Later improvements, while substantial, were incremental.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The progression from Flash Attention 1 to 4 reveals several lessons about GPU opti mization. First, algorithmic innovations matter most early on. The shift from mate rializing attention matrices to tiling and online softmax delivered the largest single speedup. Later improvements, while substantial, were incremental. Second, hardware-software co-design is increasingly important. Flash Attention 3 and 4 are inseparable from Hopper and Blackwell architectures. Their performance gains come from exploiting specific hardware features like TMA, WGMMA, and FP8 tensor cores. A kernel tuned that tightly to one chip can lose its edge on the next architecture, at other shapes, or when fewer SMs are free. Before putting that kind of work into a kernel, consider everywhere it will run, not just the one case you care about.

regions.text: Finally, this evolution shows where GPU programming is heading. Modern ker nels are becoming asynchronous, pipelined, and warp specialized. The programming model is shifting from “write a function that a thread executes” to “write a state machine where warps handle different pipeline stages.” This shift is powerful but challenging, requiring new abstractions and tools. The CUDA ecosystem is responding with libraries like CUTLASS for tensor core programming and domain-specific languages like Triton for simpler kernel authoring.

regions.text: The art of quantization is finding the right balance. Too few bits, and the noise over whelms your signal: your model’s predictions become garbage. Too many bits, and you don’t get enough memory savings to justify the added complexity. Most of the time, 8 bits hits the sweet spot: enough precision to maintain accuracy and enough compres sion to enable practical deployments.

Most of the time, 8 bits hits the sweet spot: enough precision to maintain accuracy and enough compres sion to enable practical deployments. Work through a concrete example to see how this plays out. Say we have four weights: [0.1, 0.3, 0.7, 0.9], and we want to squeeze them into just 2 bits each. With 2 bits, we get four possible values: 0, 1, 2, and 3. Our job is to map our continuous range to these four discrete levels. First, we figure out the scale: our values span from 0.1 to 0.9, a range of 0.8. We need to fit this range into four levels (0 through 3), so each level represents 0.8 / 3 ≈ 0.267 in the original scale. Now for the quantization: 0.1 divided by 0.267 gives 0.37, which rounds to 0. The value 0.3 becomes 1.12, rounding to 1. The value 0.7 becomes 2.62, rounding to 3. And 0.9 becomes 3.37, but we clamp it to 3 because that’s our maximum. When we convert back (dequantize), we get [0, 0.267, 0.8, 0.8]. Compare that to our originals [0.1, 0.3, 0.7, 0.9], and you can see the errors: we’re off by 0.1 on the first value, pretty close on the second, and off by 0.1 on the last two. The mean squared error works out to about 0.0078. That’s the price of at 2 bits. At 8 bits the step would be 0.8 / 255 ≈ 0.003, about 85 times finer.

regions.text: The diagram shows how few bins create a coarse staircase approximation of smooth data. With only 16 bins (4 bits), you can see significant gaps between the discrete lev els and the actual values. This is quantization noise in action: the difference between where you want to be and where you’re forced to land. The art of quantization is finding the right balance. Too few bits, and the noise over whelms your signal: your model’s predictions become garbage. Too many bits, and you don’t get enough memory savings to justify the added complexity. Most of the time, 8 bits hits the sweet spot: enough precision to maintain accuracy and enough compres sion to enable practical deployments. Work through a concrete example to see how this plays out. Say we have four weights: [0.1, 0.3, 0.7, 0.9], and we want to squeeze them into just 2 bits each. With 2 bits, we get four possible values: 0, 1, 2, and 3. Our job is to map our continuous range to these four discrete levels. First, we figure out the scale: our values span from 0.1 to 0.9, a range of 0.8. We need to fit this range into four levels (0 through 3), so each level represents 0.8 / 3 ≈ 0.267 in the original scale. Now for the quantization: 0.1 divided by 0.267 gives 0.37, which rounds to 0. The value 0.3 becomes 1.12, rounding to 1. The value 0.7 becomes 2.62, rounding to 3. And 0.9 becomes 3.37, but we clamp it to 3 because that’s our maximum. When we convert back (dequantize), we get [0, 0.267, 0.8, 0.8]. Compare that to our originals [0.1, 0.3, 0.7, 0.9], and you can see the errors: we’re off by 0.1 on the first value, pretty close on the second, and off by 0.1 on the last two. The mean squared error works out to about 0.0078. That’s the price of at 2 bits. At 8 bits the step would be 0.8 / 255 ≈ 0.003, about 85 times finer.

regions.label: reference
regions.text: S ymmetric and asymmetric range placement Now we need to talk about a subtle but important choice: how should you map your floating-point numbers to integers? The obvious answer might seem to be “Just use integers from –128 to 127,” but the right range depends on the shape of your data. A simple contrast makes the tradeoff clear. Suppose your weights range from −2.5 to +2.5. Symmetric INT8 is a natural fit: your scale is 2.5 / 127 ≈ 0.0197, zero maps to integer 0, –2.5 maps to –127, and +2.5 maps to +127. You use the signed range efficiently because the data is already centered around zero. Now switch to activations after a ReLU. If those activations range from 0 to 5 and you still use symmetric INT8, the integers from –128 to –1 never get used. Half your precision is wasted on values that do not exist. Asymmetric quantization fixes that by shifting the usable range to where the data actually lies. In this case, 0 maps to 0, 5 maps to 255, and every integer in between carries useful signal. Figure 9.3 shows the difference. This ability to move the range around is a major advantage of integer quantization. Figure 9.4 shows why.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Now we need to talk about a subtle but important choice: how should you map your floating-point numbers to integers? The obvious answer might seem to be “Just use integers from –128 to 127,” but the right range depends on the shape of your data. A simple contrast makes the tradeoff clear. Suppose your weights range from −2.5 to +2.5. Symmetric INT8 is a natural fit: your scale is 2.5 / 127 ≈ 0.0197, zero maps to integer 0, –2.5 maps to –127, and +2.5 maps to +127. You use the signed range efficiently because the data is already centered around zero.

regions.text: Now we need to talk about a subtle but important choice: how should you map your floating-point numbers to integers? The obvious answer might seem to be “Just use integers from –128 to 127,” but the right range depends on the shape of your data. A simple contrast makes the tradeoff clear. Suppose your weights range from −2.5 to +2.5. Symmetric INT8 is a natural fit: your scale is 2.5 / 127 ≈ 0.0197, zero maps to integer 0, –2.5 maps to –127, and +2.5 maps to +127. You use the signed range efficiently because the data is already centered around zero. Now switch to activations after a ReLU. If those activations range from 0 to 5 and you still use symmetric INT8, the integers from –128 to –1 never get used. Half your precision is wasted on values that do not exist. Asymmetric quantization fixes that by shifting the usable range to where the data actually lies. In this case, 0 maps to 0, 5 maps to 255, and every integer in between carries useful signal. regions.label: text
regions.text: With integer quantization, you have complete control over where your zero point sits and how your scale factor maps to the data distribution. The two number lines show the same integer format aimed at two different regions of the real line: slide the zero point and stretch or shrink the scale, and your limited set of integer levels lands exactly where your data lives. Floating point offers no such knob. Its layout is fixed by the format itself: dense near zero and sparse far from it, whether or not that matches your data.

The two number lines show the same integer format aimed at two different regions of the real line: slide the zero point and stretch or shrink the scale, and your limited set of integer levels lands exactly where your data lives. Floating point offers no such knob. Its layout is fixed by the format itself: dense near zero and sparse far from it, whether or not that matches your data. But floating-point formats such as FP8, FP16, and FP4 fix the exponent/signifi cand split inside each value, and they always place zero at exactly zero: there is no additive zero point to slide the way affine integer quantization has. In practice, FP8 and FP4 recipes recover the missing range knob by attaching external scale factors (per-tensor scaling in Transformer Engine, per-block scales in MXFP4/NVFP4); what the format itself fixes is the shape of the value spacing, dense near zero and sparse far from it.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Floating-point numbers split their bits among sign, exponent, and significand fields. The exponent sets the rough order of magnitude on a logarithmic scale, while the significand, historically called the mantissa , fills in the fine detail within that range. Because those field widths are fixed by the format, FP8 and FP16 cannot slide their dynamic range around to match your data the way integer quantization can.

regions.label: text
regions.text: At its heart, quantization is just division, rounding, and clamping. Your FP32 value is divided by a scale factor, rounded to the nearest integer, and clamped to fit within your target integer range. Dequantization reverses this process: multiply by the scale factor to get back to floating point. Every thing comes down to choosing that scale fac tor wisely and applying it at the right level of detail.

regions.text: Say we have four weights: [1.2, –0.8, 2.5, –1.7]. Before we can quantize them, we need the scale factor. For symmetric quantization, we take the maximum absolute value (2.5 in this case) and divide it by 127: scale = 2.5 / 127 ≈ 0.0197. We divide by 127 because INT8 ranges from –128 to +127, and we want our maximum value to map exactly to +127, not overflow into –128.

regions.text: Each thread handles one element independently: classic embarrassingly parallel work. Divide by the scale, clamp to the valid range, round to the nearest integer, and write it out. The clamping step is critical: without it, a value that’s slightly too large could over flow and wrap around to a large negative number, catastrophically corrupting your weights.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Going back is even simpler. To dequantize, you just multiply by that same scale factor: dequantized = quantized * scale . No rounding is needed because you’re converting from integer to float, and the float has enough precision to exactly represent any 8-bit integer.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Take our quantized values [61, –41, 127, –86] and a scale of 0.0197. Multiply each by the scale: 61 × 0.0197 ≈ 1.20. Then, –41 × 0.0197 ≈ –0.81. Our maximum is 127 × 0.0197 ≈ 2.50, and –86 × 0.0197 ≈ –1.69.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Compare these values to our originals [1.2, –0.8, 2.5, –1.7], and you can see the quan tization noise: the first value has zero error, the second is off by 0.01, the third has zero error, and the fourth is off by 0.01. These tiny errors are the price we pay for 4× com pression. For most neural network computations, these errors are well within the mod el’s noise tolerance.

regions.label: text
regions.text: You need to validate the quantization quality, and there are two perspectives to con sider: error metrics and task performance. Mean squared error (MSE) squares each error before averaging, which means it heavily penalizes outliers. If you quantize 1,000 values perfectly but completely butcher one value, MSE will be dominated by that sin gle bad value. This is useful because those outliers often cause the worst problems in practice. Mean absolute error (MAE) averages the absolute values of the errors. It’s more intuitive: it tells you the typical size of the error you should expect on any given value. For our running example with errors [0.0, –0.01, 0.0, –0.01], the MAE is 0.005; on average, we’re off by half a hundredth.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Choosing a low-precision format is only the first half of the problem. You also have to decide how broadly each quantization parameter gets reused: one scale for an entire tensor, one per output feature, or one per local block. That reuse pattern determines both the quantization error and the amount of bookkeeping your ker nels must carry.
