regions.label: text
regions.text: Now we hit the real design question: do you use one scale factor for the entire tensor or different scale factors for different parts? This choice has profound implications for both accuracy and efficiency.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Think about a typical weight matrix in a transformer. Maybe it’s 4096 × 4096—about

regions.label: text
regions.text: Think about a typical weight matrix in a transformer. Maybe it’s 4096 × 4096—about 67 million parameters. You could compute one scale factor by finding the maximum absolute value across all 67 million weights, then quantize everything using that single scale. This is simple and efficient but potentially wasteful. What if one column of the matrix has weights ranging from –2.5 to +2.5, while another column ranges from just –0.1 to +0.1? With a single scale factor tuned for the larger range, you’d be squandering precision on that smaller-range column.

regions.label: text

regions.label: text
regions.text: Or you could compute a different scale for each column: 4,096 different scales. Now each column gets quantized according to its own range, maximizing precision every

regions.label: text
regions.text: Or you could compute a different scale for each column: 4,096 different scales. Now each column gets quantized according to its own range, maximizing precision every where. But you’ve added 4,096 scale factors to your model, and your kernel needs to look up the correct scale for each column it processes. The code gets more complex, the memory footprint grows, and the kernel might slow down.

regions.label: text
regions.text: But the accuracy gains are often worth it. Convolutional networks benefit enor mously because different channels learn completely different features, such as edge detectors, color detectors, and texture patterns, with wildly varying magnitudes. Trans former attention and feed-forward layers show similar patterns. If your features have heterogeneous ranges, channel-wise quantization substantially reduces quantization error compared to tensor-wise quantization, and the accuracy gap grows with how much the per-channel ranges differ.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Figure 9.8 shows how grouping bal ances precision and overhead. Instead of one scale per channel, you group adjacent channels together. Maybe every 64 or 128 channels share a scale. For that 4,096-output weight matrix, you’d compute 4,096/128 = 32 scales instead of 4,096. You get most of the benefits of channel-wise quantization (adapting to local feature statistics) at a frac tion of the memory cost.

regions.label: number
regions.text: This shows up constantly in large language model quantization. When you have weight matrices with tens of thousands of columns, storing a scale per column adds up fast. But grouping 128 columns together keeps the scale overhead to a few per cent of the quantized model size (one FP16 scale per 128 INT4 weights is about 3%), while still capturing the variation across features. Group sizes of 64 or 128 have become standard in practice (AWQ and GPTQ both default to 128; QLoRA uses 64)—small enough to adapt to local statistics but large enough to keep overhead minimal.

regions.text: Block-wise quantization divides the spatial dimen sions into blocks, as illustrated in figure 9.9. Each block gets its own scale. Imagine a 32 × 32 feature map—you might use 4 × 4 blocks, giving you 64 dif ferent scales across the spatial extent. This captures local spatial statistics: if part of an image is bright and high contrast while another part is dark and low con trast, each region gets quantized appropriately.

regions.label: number
regions.text: 9.2.2 Calibration: Computing quantization parameters Everything we’ve built so far assumes you have good scale factors. But where do those scales come from? You can’t compute them from your test data during inference—that would defeat the entire point of static quantization. You need to precompute them from representative data, a process called calibration . Get this wrong, and even the clev erest quantization scheme will fail. This is also where the earlier feature and channel language becomes concrete. Cal ibration computes one scale for each slice you decided to reuse during inference: one for the whole tensor in tensor-wise quantization, one per output feature in channel-wise quantization, one per group in group-wise quantization, and so on.

regions.text: P ercentile calibration Percentile calibration offers a more robust alternative: instead of using the absolute minimum and maximum, it uses percentiles. Set your scale based on, say, the 99th per centile of your data. This means you intentionally clip the most extreme 1% of values but optimize your quantization range for the other 99%. Those outlier values—the extreme activations that occur rarely—often don’t matter much to your model’s final predictions. Yes, you’re clipping them, but if they’re statisti cal flukes or numerical instabilities, your model has likely learned to be robust to them anyway. By ignoring them during calibration, you concentrate your limited quantiza tion precision on the values that actually occur frequently.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Percentile calibration offers a more robust alternative: instead of using the absolute minimum and maximum, it uses percentiles. Set your scale based on, say, the 99th per centile of your data. This means you intentionally clip the most extreme 1% of values but optimize your quantization range for the other 99%. Those outlier values—the extreme activations that occur rarely—often don’t matter much to your model’s final predictions. Yes, you’re clipping them, but if they’re statisti cal flukes or numerical instabilities, your model has likely learned to be robust to them anyway. By ignoring them during calibration, you concentrate your limited quantiza tion precision on the values that actually occur frequently.

regions.text: Let’s revisit our problematic example, [0.1, 0.5, 0.8, 100.0], but now with a larger data set. Say you have 1,000 values: 990 of them range from 0 to 5, and 10 are outliers around 100. The 99th percentile is somewhere around 5. Set your scale based on 0 to 5, and now those 990 normal values get the full quantization range. The 10 outliers get clamped to your maximum quantization level, but that’s fine; they were probably anomalies anyway.

regions.text: set. Say you have 1,000 values: 990 of them range from 0 to 5, and 10 are outliers around 100. The 99th percentile is somewhere around 5. Set your scale based on 0 to 5, and now those 990 normal values get the full quantization range. The 10 outliers get clamped to your maximum quantization level, but that’s fine; they were probably anomalies anyway. For symmetric quantization, you often use the 95th or 99th percentile of absolute val ues. This means you’re finding a value V such that 95% or 99% of your data falls within [–V, V], then setting your scale based on V rather than the true maximum. The choice of percentile is a knob you can tune: the 99th percentile is aggressive about excluding outliers; the 99.9th percentile is more conservative. The right choice depends on how clean your data is and how much clipping you can tolerate. Percentile calibration does introduce one complication: you need to compute per centiles, which is slower than just finding the max. For static quantization, where cali bration happens once during model conversion, this is usually fine, but it’s something to be aware of.

regions.label: text
regions.text: T he effect of calibration quality Bad calibration can damage your model more than aggressive quantization ever could. If you quantize to 4 bits with perfect calibration, you might lose 2% accuracy. If you quantize to 8 bits with terrible calibration, you might lose 20% accuracy. The scale fac tors matter that much. This is why you should always validate calibration on separate test data. Don’t mea sure quantization error on your calibration set; that’s circular. Run your quantized model on data it hasn’t seen, and measure both the quantization error (MSE/MAE) and the downstream task metric (accuracy, perplexity, or whatever you care about). If calibration is failing, you have several levers to pull. Collect more calibration samples: maybe your current set isn’t representative. Try different percentile thresh olds: maybe the 99th percentile is too aggressive and you should use 99.9th percentile. Switch from tensor-wise to channel-wise calibration to capture per-feature statistics. Or manually filter your calibration data to remove known-bad examples. Calibration is an empirical search for the scale factors that work best for your specific model and data distribution. With reliable calibration methods in hand, the next question is when to compute those scales: predeployment or at runtime.

regions.text: There are two things to notice. First is the callout 3 trick: CUDA has no atomicMax for floats, but for nonnegative floats, the raw bit patterns sort in the same order as the values, so an integer atomicMax on the bits gives the exact float maximum. Second, there is no pass-two listing because you already have it: the host reads back the stored maximum, divides by 127 to get the scale, and launches the exact same quantize_ fp32_to_int8 kernel from the previous section with that scale. Static and dynamic quantization share the quantize kernel; the only difference is where the scale came from. One came from calibration data last week; the other came from this batch a microsecond ago.

regions.text: There are two things to notice. First is the callout 3 trick: CUDA has no atomicMax for floats, but for nonnegative floats, the raw bit patterns sort in the same order as the values, so an integer atomicMax on the bits gives the exact float maximum. Second, there is no pass-two listing because you already have it: the host reads back the stored maximum, divides by 127 to get the scale, and launches the exact same quantize_ fp32_to_int8 kernel from the previous section with that scale. Static and dynamic quantization share the quantize kernel; the only difference is where the scale came from. One came from calibration data last week; the other came from this batch a microsecond ago. The cost is obvious: you’re doing extra computation during the forward pass. Before you can proceed with the actual layer computation, you need to gather statistics over all the activations. On a GPU, this requires a reduction kernel to find the maximum absolute value, which adds latency. The exact overhead depends on tensor size, reuse pattern, and hardware, but it is never free. Dynamic quantization is worth it when your input distribution is genuinely variable and you can’t calibrate for the worst case without wasting precision on the common case. Research prototypes often use dynamic quantization because you’re still explor ing the input space. Applications with truly diverse inputs, such as multimodal models, content moderation, and medical imaging with different scan types benefit from the adaptability. And if your batch size is small (say, batch size 1 for interactive applica tions), the per-batch overhead matters less because you’re not amortizing it over many examples. Match your quantization strategy to your deployment constraints. If you can get away with static, you should, because it’s faster. If your accuracy suffers too much from static’s rigid scales, dynamic gives you an escape hatch at the cost of performance.

regions.label: text
regions.text: That sounds backward at first: shouldn’t you shrink the thing you want to protect? But remember how quantization error works. Every weight in a group gets rounded with the same step size, set by the largest weight in the group. Rounding costs each weight up to half a step, no matter how big or small the weight is. So a weight’s rounding error is fixed; what varies is how much that error gets amplified when it hits the activa tion. Scale the weight up by s and the activation down by s , and the rounding error now gets multiplied by an activation that’s s times smaller. The error that reaches the output shrinks by s . That’s the whole mechanism.

regions.text: 9.4 Putting it all together A practical quantization workflow combines choices that balance accuracy, perfor mance, and complexity.

regions.label: number
regions.text: 9.4.1 Real model quantization workflow Start with granularity. For transformer attention layers, different heads often have dif ferent output scales, so channel-wise quantization makes sense: compute one scale per head. For massive feed-forward networks, you might have 4096 × 4096 weight matri ces, where channel-wise quantization means 4,096 scales, adding noticeable overhead. Here, group-wise quantization with groups of 128 gives you 32 scales per row: enough granularity to capture variation, with overhead small enough to be practical. Table 9.1 summarizes the granularity that fits each kind of tensor. Next, calibration. You need representative data that spans the distribution your model will see in production. Gather about 1,000 diverse examples, run them through your model, and observe the activation ranges. Use percentile-based calibration, per haps the 99.9th percentile, for robustness against outliers. Those few weird examples with enormous activations shouldn’t dictate your scales for everyone else.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Start with granularity. For transformer attention layers, different heads often have dif ferent output scales, so channel-wise quantization makes sense: compute one scale per head. For massive feed-forward networks, you might have 4096 × 4096 weight matri ces, where channel-wise quantization means 4,096 scales, adding noticeable overhead. Here, group-wise quantization with groups of 128 gives you 32 scales per row: enough granularity to capture variation, with overhead small enough to be practical. Table 9.1 summarizes the granularity that fits each kind of tensor.

regions.label: footer
regions.text: Now choose symmetric versus asymmetric. Your weights came from training with proper initialization, so they’re centered around zero. Use symmetric INT8 quanti zation. But your activations flow through ReLU layers, creating positive-only distribu tions. Use asymmetric UINT8 for those. PyTorch’s eager-mode recipe uses this pairing, while TensorRT quantizes both symmetrically. For deployment mode, static quantization is your default. Compute your scales during the model conversion process and bake them into the checkpoint. Reach for dynamic quantization only if you discover that your input distribution varies so wildly that static scales hurt accuracy. If you’re doing weight-only quantization (keeping activations in FP32 or FP16 but quantizing weights to save memory), consider AWQ. The weight transformation hap pens once during model conversion, and it can significantly improve quantization qual ity without adding runtime cost. Finally, implement your pipeline. Start with the basic quantize and dequantize ker nels we developed earlier. Add support for your chosen granularity, loading the right scale for each channel or group. Integrate your calibration code to compute scales from your calibration dataset. Wire it all together into a model conversion tool that takes an FP32 checkpoint and produces a quantized version. For that typical transformer, you’d end up with something like this: attention lay ers using channel-wise symmetric static quantization, feed-forward networks using group-wise symmetric static quantization, layer norms using tensor-wise quantization (they’re small and stable), and embeddings using channel-wise asymmetric quantiza tion if they’re skewed. Calibrate on 1,000 diverse samples with percentile-based ranges. Against the FP32 checkpoint, INT8 weights take 4× less memory. The speedup and accuracy loss depend on the model, so measure both as the next section describes.

regions.label: footer
regions.text: 9.4.2 Accuracy validation strategy You’ve made all these choices—granularity, calibration method, symmetric versus asymmetric. Now you need to know whether they actually work. This requires compre hensive evaluation across multiple dimensions.

If your quantized model performs well on calibration data but poorly on vali dation data, your calibration wasn’t representative enough. Track both error metrics and task performance. MSE tells you the average quantiza tion error across all your parameters, which is useful for debugging, but what you really care about is downstream performance. For a language model, measure perplexity or next-token prediction accuracy. For an image classifier, measure top-1 accuracy. For object detection, measure mean average precision (mAP). These task-specific metrics tell you whether your users will notice the quantization.

regions.text: And finally, don’t overengineer from the start. Begin with simple tensor-wise, min max, static quantization. Measure the results. If accuracy is good enough, you’re done. If not, identify the specific problem (outliers? varying feature scales? distri bution shift?) and apply the appropriate advanced technique. AWQ and group-wise quantization are powerful but add complexity, so reach for them only when simpler approaches fail.

regions.text: The first choice is bit width, and it’s really a memory budget question. INT8 buys you 4× compression and, with good calibration, near-zero accuracy loss: it’s the safe default. INT4 buys 8× compression, but the noise is no longer negligible, so it almost never travels alone: it brings group-wise scales and usually a protection scheme like AWQ or GPTQ along with it. If INT8 fits your hardware and your latency target, stop there. The second choice is where zero lives. Symmetric quantization is simpler: no zero point to store, no offset arithmetic in the kernel, and it’s the right call for weights, which training keeps centered around zero. Asymmetric quantization costs you that extra off set but stops you from wasting half the integer range on values that never occur, which is exactly the situation ReLU activations put you in. The tradeoff is a little kernel com plexity for a lot of recovered precision, it’s why PyTorch’s eager-mode recipe quantizes weights symmetrically and activations asymmetrically. The third choice is how many scales to keep. One scale per tensor is nearly free but lets a single outlier ruin precision for millions of well-behaved values. One scale per channel, or per group of 128, contains the damage locally, at the cost of storing and load ing more metadata. The finer you slice, the better each slice fits its data, and the more overhead you carry: granularity is the dial that trades accuracy against bookkeeping. The fourth choice is when scales get computed. Static quantization computes them once from calibration data and pays nothing at inference time, but it’s a bet that tomor row’s inputs will look like the calibration set. Dynamic quantization recomputes the scale per batch—a reduction pass before every quantized layer—and in exchange, it never gets caught by a distribution it hasn’t seen. You’re trading latency for robustness, and the hon est way to decide is to measure static quantization’s accuracy on your worst-case inputs first. The last choice is whether to spend effort protecting the weights that matter most. Plain rounding treats every weight as equally important; AWQ uses calibration activa tions to find the weights whose errors get amplified the most and shifts scale onto them before rounding, all at conversion time, with zero inference cost. The cost is pipeline complexity and the need for decent calibration data. None of these choices is exotic on its own. regions.text: What makes it fast is giving up the careful pick-the-next-weight ordering of earlier methods (the fixed shared order turns out to cost little accuracy at scale) and batch- processing 128 columns at once to keep the GPU busy. The weights are stored as INT4 (4 bits), but the clever part is that they’re converted back to FP16 on the fly during inference in the same kernel that uses them. You get 4× memory savings because INT4 weights stay compressed until the exact moment you multiply them.

Neural network weights aren’t uniformly distributed; they follow roughly a normal (Gaussian) distribution centered around zero. Most weights cluster near zero, with fewer weights at the extremes. Traditional uniform quantization wastes precious quan tization levels on ranges where few weights actually live. NF4 fixes this by deriving its quantization levels from the quantiles of a standard normal distribution. The QLoRA authors describe the result as information-theoretically optimal for normally distrib uted weights; later analysis showed it is not exactly optimal, but it is close, and it works well in practice.

regions.label: footer
regions.text: Here’s how it works: NF4 uses 16 fixed quantization levels (4 bits), but unlike uni form quantization, where levels are evenly spaced, NF4’s levels cluster densely around zero, where most weights live, with sparser coverage at the extremes. The quantization process operates block-wise (typically 64 weights per block). For each block, find the maximum absolute value (absmax), normalize all weights by this value to the range [–1, 1], and then map each normalized weight to its closest NF4 level. Store the 4-bit index and the absmax scale factor. Dequantization reverses this process: look up the NF4 level from the 4-bit index, multiply it by the stored absmax, and you recover the approximate original weight. What makes NF4 particularly powerful is double quantization: the absmax scale fac tors themselves are quantized to save even more memory. Because you have one scale per block, and typical models have millions of blocks, those scales add up. Quantizing them (typically to 8-bit) provides additional compression with minimal accuracy loss. NF4 shines in QLoRA, where the entire pre-trained base model is quantized to NF4 and frozen, while small trainable LoRA adapters stay in bfloat16 . This lets you fine tune 65B-parameter models on a single 48 GB GPU, or 70B-parameter models on dual consumer GPUs, something impossible with full-precision weights. The base model’s 4-bit weights are dequantized to bfloat16 just in time during computation, but they stay compressed in memory. The results are impressive: QLoRA reports that 4-bit NF4 fine-tuning matches full 16-bit fine-tuning task performance, while using 4× less memory than 16-bit and 8× less than 32-bit.

regions.label: footer
regions.text: 9.5.3 Quantization-aware training All the techniques we’ve covered are posttraining quantization—you train your model normally, then quantize afterwards. Quantization-aware training (QAT) takes the opposite approach: include quantization effects during training itself. The idea is to simulate quantization during forward passes. Your weights are stored in full precision, but during the forward pass, you quantize them, use the quantized values for computation, and then backpropagate gradients as if the rounding didn’t happen. The model learns which weight values survive quantization well and adjusts during training so that it is robust to quantization noise from the start. QAT can achieve remarkable results: models that maintain accuracy even at 4-bit precision or lower. But there’s a cost: you need to retrain (or at least fine-tune) your entire model, which is expensive. You also need to carefully tune hyperparameters to balance quantization effects with normal training. For production models where you have the compute budget and accuracy is paramount, QAT is worth considering. But for most use cases, post-training quantization with good calibration gets you 90% of the way there at a fraction of the cost.

regions.text: form quantization, where levels are evenly spaced, NF4’s levels cluster densely around zero, where most weights live, with sparser coverage at the extremes. The quantization process operates block-wise (typically 64 weights per block). For each block, find the maximum absolute value (absmax), normalize all weights by this value to the range [–1, 1], and then map each normalized weight to its closest NF4 level. Store the 4-bit index and the absmax scale factor. Dequantization reverses this process: look up the NF4 level from the 4-bit index, multiply it by the stored absmax, and you recover the approximate original weight. What makes NF4 particularly powerful is double quantization: the absmax scale fac tors themselves are quantized to save even more memory. Because you have one scale per block, and typical models have millions of blocks, those scales add up. Quantizing them (typically to 8-bit) provides additional compression with minimal accuracy loss. NF4 shines in QLoRA, where the entire pre-trained base model is quantized to NF4 and frozen, while small trainable LoRA adapters stay in bfloat16 . This lets you fine tune 65B-parameter models on a single 48 GB GPU, or 70B-parameter models on dual consumer GPUs, something impossible with full-precision weights. The base model’s 4-bit weights are dequantized to bfloat16 just in time during computation, but they stay compressed in memory. The results are impressive: QLoRA reports that 4-bit NF4 fine-tuning matches full 16-bit fine-tuning task performance, while using 4× less memory than 16-bit and 8× less than 32-bit.

regions.label: text
regions.text: 9.5.3 Quantization-aware training All the techniques we’ve covered are posttraining quantization—you train your model normally, then quantize afterwards. Quantization-aware training (QAT) takes the opposite approach: include quantization effects during training itself. The idea is to simulate quantization during forward passes. Your weights are stored in full precision, but during the forward pass, you quantize them, use the quantized values for computation, and then backpropagate gradients as if the rounding didn’t happen. The model learns which weight values survive quantization well and adjusts during training so that it is robust to quantization noise from the start. QAT can achieve remarkable results: models that maintain accuracy even at 4-bit precision or lower. But there’s a cost: you need to retrain (or at least fine-tune) your entire model, which is expensive. You also need to carefully tune hyperparameters to balance quantization effects with normal training. For production models where you have the compute budget and accuracy is paramount, QAT is worth considering. But for most use cases, post-training quantization with good calibration gets you 90% of the way there at a fraction of the cost.

You can benchmark NCCL performance using the nccl-tests suite. On an 8-GPU H100 system with NVLink, you should see aggregate AllReduce bus bandwidth ( busbw ) of roughly 450 to 480 GB/s for large messages, corresponding to about 270 GB/s of algorithm bandwidth. That is the ceiling for large messages on that node. Small mes sages land far below it because per-step latency dominates. NCCL provides collective operations, including AllReduce, Broadcast, Reduce, AllGather, ReduceScatter, AllToAll, Gather, and Scatter; we focus on the ones distrib uted training leans on most heavily. Each serves a specific communication pattern that appears repeatedly in distributed deep learning. We’ll cover the theory of each opera tion here; the actual implementations are handled by NCCL’s highly optimized kernels.

regions.text: AllReduce is the workhorse of distributed training. The name tells you exactly what it does: it reduces (combines) data from all GPUs and then gives the result to all GPUs. Here’s the concrete scenario: you have four GPUs, and each GPU has computed a partial result. Maybe GPU 0 computed gradients from its batch of training data and got the value 1. GPU 1 got 2, GPU 2 got 3, and GPU 3 got 4. You want to combine these partial results by summing them (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10) and then give that final result (10) to every GPU. That’s exactly what AllReduce does. The “reduce” part means we apply an operation to combine the values. The most common operation is sum, but you can also use max, min, or product. The “all” part means every GPU gets the final result. This is different from a regular reduce operation, where only one GPU gets the answer. In data-parallel training, each GPU processes a different batch of data and computes gradients. But you want all GPUs to update their weights using the average gradient across all batches. AllReduce with sum gives you the total gradient, which you then divide by the number of GPUs to get the average. Each GPU performs this AllReduce after its backward pass, and then each GPU has the same averaged gradients to update its local copy of the model. regions.label: abstract
regions.text: does: it reduces (combines) data from all GPUs and then gives the result to all GPUs. Here’s the concrete scenario: you have four GPUs, and each GPU has computed a partial result. Maybe GPU 0 computed gradients from its batch of training data and got the value 1. GPU 1 got 2, GPU 2 got 3, and GPU 3 got 4. You want to combine these partial results by summing them (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10) and then give that final result (10) to every GPU. That’s exactly what AllReduce does. The “reduce” part means we apply an operation to combine the values. The most common operation is sum, but you can also use max, min, or product. The “all” part means every GPU gets the final result. This is different from a regular reduce operation, where only one GPU gets the answer. In data-parallel training, each GPU processes a different batch of data and computes gradients. But you want all GPUs to update their weights using the average gradient across all batches. AllReduce with sum gives you the total gradient, which you then divide by the number of GPUs to get the average. Each GPU performs this AllReduce after its backward pass, and then each GPU has the same averaged gradients to update its local copy of the model. In tensor parallelism, we saw this in action: each GPU computed a partial matrix mul tiplication result, and AllReduce summed the results to give every GPU the complete output matrix. In distributed batch normalization, you’d use AllReduce to compute the mean and variance across all GPUs’ data, not just one GPU’s batch. Two costs matter, and it helps to keep them separate. The first is bytes: with NCCL’s ring algorithm, each GPU sends and receives about 2N bytes in total (2(P–1)/P × N, to be exact), where N is the size of the data being reduced. That bandwidth term is O(N) and barely changes as you add GPUs. The second is steps: the ring needs 2(P–1) sequential steps for P GPUs, so the latency term grows with P. For a model with 1 billion parameters, that’s 4 GB of data at FP32 precision, and on an 8-GPU NVLink system the whole operation takes about 16 ms (measured with nccl-tests on an 8× H100 SXM node: 15.8 ms, a bus bandwidth of 476 GB/s).

regions.text: roadcast B Broadcast is simpler than AllReduce. One GPU has some data, and you want to copy that exact data to every other GPU. There’s no combining and no reduction—just copying. Say GPU 0 has the original data, and GPUs 1, 2, and 3 are receivers who each get an identical copy. After the broadcast, all four GPUs have exactly the same data. Figure 10.2 shows this one-to-many pattern. When do you need this? At the start of training, you typically initialize the model weights on one GPU (maybe GPU 0 loads them from a checkpoint file). The “reduce” part means we apply an operation to combine the values. The most common operation is sum, but you can also use max, min, or product. The “all” part means every GPU gets the final result. This is different from a regular reduce operation, where only one GPU gets the answer. In data-parallel training, each GPU processes a different batch of data and computes gradients. But you want all GPUs to update their weights using the average gradient across all batches. AllReduce with sum gives you the total gradient, which you then divide by the number of GPUs to get the average. Each GPU performs this AllReduce after its backward pass, and then each GPU has the same averaged gradients to update its local copy of the model. In tensor parallelism, we saw this in action: each GPU computed a partial matrix mul tiplication result, and AllReduce summed the results to give every GPU the complete output matrix. In distributed batch normalization, you’d use AllReduce to compute the mean and variance across all GPUs’ data, not just one GPU’s batch. Two costs matter, and it helps to keep them separate. The first is bytes: with NCCL’s ring algorithm, each GPU sends and receives about 2N bytes in total (2(P–1)/P × N, to be exact), where N is the size of the data being reduced. That bandwidth term is O(N) and barely changes as you add GPUs. The second is steps: the ring needs 2(P–1) sequential steps for P GPUs, so the latency term grows with P. For a model with 1 billion parameters, that’s 4 GB of data at FP32 precision, and on an 8-GPU NVLink system the whole operation takes about 16 ms (measured with nccl-tests on an 8× H100 SXM node: 15.8 ms, a bus bandwidth of 476 GB/s).

regions.label: text
regions.text: Why is this useful? In FSDP, each GPU is responsible for updating a different shard of the model parameters. After computing gradients, you need to average them across GPUs, but each GPU only needs the averaged gradients for its own shard. Reduce Scatter does exactly this: it computes the averaged gradients and gives each GPU only the piece it needs. This saves memory because no GPU has to store the full gradient array.

regions.label: text
regions.text: This is the key operation in FSDP. Remember how FSDP shards model parameters across GPUs to save memory? When GPU 0 needs to run a forward pass through a layer, it needs the complete layer weights, not just its shard. So it calls AllGather to tem porarily reconstruct the full weights from all the shards. GPU 0 contributes its shard A, GPU 1 contributes shard B, and so on. After AllGather, all GPUs have the com plete layer weights and can compute the forward pass. Then they discard the gathered weights to free memory.

If you combine ReduceScatter and AllGather, you get AllReduce. ReduceScatter computes partial sums and distributes them, then AllGather collects those partial sums and gives everyone the complete result. NCCL actually implements AllReduce this way internally for large messages, using the ring algorithm to make both stages efficient.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The tree algorithm arranges GPUs in a logical binary tree. During reduction, data flows up from the leaves to the root: each leaf sends its value to a parent node, which sums the inputs and passes the result one level higher. Figure 10.8 shows this process with four GPUs. Values [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] combine into partial sums at the intermediate nodes, and the root ends up with the total.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The problem is this: multiply a 4096 × 4096 input matrix by a 4096 × 4096 weight matrix. At FP16 precision, that’s 32 MB for the input, 32 MB for the weights, and 32 MB for the output. That fits easily on one GPU. But imagine scaling to 16384 × 16384 matrices. Now we’re at 512 MB each, and we haven’t even loaded the actual model yet. Or consider a real transformer: today’s large dense models use hidden dimensions of 8,192 to 16,384, so a single projection matrix can be 12288 × 12288 or bigger. One such matrix is about 302 MB at FP16, but a model built from hundreds of them, like GPT-3 at 350 GB, needs multiple GPUs.

regions.text: The solution is tensor parallelism. We split the weight matrix by rows across eight GPUs, so each GPU gets 1/8 of the rows (a 512 × 4096 shard), and we split the input matrix by columns to match (a 4096 × 512 shard). Each GPU multiplies its input slice

regions.label: text
regions.text: The solution is tensor parallelism. We split the weight matrix by rows across eight GPUs, so each GPU gets 1/8 of the rows (a 512 × 4096 shard), and we split the input matrix by columns to match (a 4096 × 512 shard). Each GPU multiplies its input slice by its weight shard. Because the split runs along the inner (K) dimension of the matrix multiplication, each GPU’s product is a full-size 4096 × 4096 matrix that contains 1/8 of every output element’s inner product: a partial sum. Then we use AllReduce to sum the partial outputs across GPUs, giving each GPU the complete result. Figure 10.10 shows the sharding pattern.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The first step in any distributed program is identifying which process you are and which GPU you should use. We use message passing interface (MPI) for this. We use processes rather than threads because the one-process-per-GPU model isolates device state and gives each GPU a clear rank. MPI starts and numbers those processes and lets them exchange small setup messages. The heavy tensor traffic between GPUs is NCCL’s job.

regions.text: The input memory per GPU shrinks by a factor of 8. That is the point of tensor parallelism: for matrices too large for one GPU, each GPU stores and touches only its own shard. The output buffer stays full size because AllReduce leaves every GPU holding the complete result, ready to feed the next layer without any further data movement.

regions.label: reference
regions.text: Read that last line again: on eight GPUs, this tensor-parallel multiply is slower than run ning the whole thing on one GPU. The result is correct (the verification against an FP32 reference passes, with FP16-level error), each GPU sustains around 510 TFLOPS on its shard, and the compute really did drop by 8×, from 0.177 ms to 0.034 ms. But the AllReduce takes about 0.19 ms regardless, because it has to move the full 4096 × 4096 output no matter how thin the K slices are, and at this problem size, communication accounts for 84% of the step. This is the single most important measurement in the chapter. Tensor parallelism is first a memory strategy: it lets you run layers whose weights do not fit on one GPU. Whether it also makes you faster depends on the ratio of compute to communication. The local GEMM does 2MNK / P FLOPs, while the AllReduce moves M × N output ele ments no matter what K is. Grow the inner dimension, and the balance shifts. Table 10.1

regions.label: text
regions.text: The advantage of pipeline parallelism is higher throughput through concurrent execution. The challenge is keeping all GPUs busy. The naive approach (process one batch at a time through the pipeline) leaves most GPUs idle. The optimized approach (use CUDA streams to process multiple batches simultaneously) achieves near-perfect utilization.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The problem is cudaDeviceSynchronize() . This blocks the CPU until the GPU fin ishes. Since we call it after every layer, we force a global ordering: GPU 0 must finish before GPU 1 starts, GPU 1 must finish before GPU 2 starts, and so on. Only one GPU is active at a time. Figure 10.13 shows the intended steady-state pipeline shape.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Adding GPUs makes things worse. We have four GPUs but get only a 1.1× speedup over a single GPU. The efficiency (speedup divided by GPU count) is 27%, meaning we’re wasting 73% of our hardware. The extra GPUs add latency (data transfer overhead) without adding throughput.

regions.label: paragraph_title
regions.title: 10.3.2 Optimized implementation: CUDA streams
regions.text: 10.3.2 Optimized implementation: CUDA streams

regions.label: text
regions.text: 10.3.2 Optimized implementation: CUDA streams

regions.label: text
regions.text: CUDA streams solve the concurrency problem. A stream is an independent queue of GPU operations. Operations in different streams can execute simultaneously. By assigning each batch to its own stream, we allow multiple batches to be in flight at once.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Here is the core idea:

regions.label: text
regions.text: ¡ Stream 0 processes batch 0 (GPU 0 → GPU 1 → GPU 2 → GPU 3).

regions.label: text
regions.text: Stream 0 processes batch 0 (GPU 0 → GPU 1 → GPU 2 → GPU 3).

regions.label: text
regions.text: → GPU 1 → GPU 2 → GPU 3).

regions.label: text
regions.text: ¡ Stream 1 processes batch 1 (GPU 0 → GPU 1 → GPU 2 → GPU 3).

regions.label: text
regions.text: ¡ Stream 2 processes batch 2 (GPU 0 → GPU 1 → GPU 2 → GPU 3).

regions.label: text
regions.text: → GPU 1 → GPU 2 → GPU 3).

regions.label: text
regions.text: ¡ Stream 3 processes batch 3 (GPU 0 → GPU 1 → GPU 2 → GPU 3).

regions.label: text
regions.text: While batch 0 is on GPU 1, batch 1 can start on GPU 0. While batch 0 is on GPU 2, batch 1 is on GPU 1, and batch 2 is on GPU 0. This creates a “staircase” pattern where all GPUs are working simultaneously.

regions.text: ¡ Strong scaling —Fix the problem size, add more GPUs, and measure speedup. For example: a 4096 × 4096 GEMM on one GPU takes 1 ms. On eight GPUs, how long does it take? If it takes 0.125 ms (1/8), that’s perfect strong scaling. If it takes 0.2 ms, that’s a 5× speedup (62.5% efficiency).

regions.label: text
regions.text: ¡ Strong scaling example —In the pipeline parallelism test, we processed 256 batches of size 64 (a fixed problem). With one GPU, throughput was ~600,000 samples/s. With four GPUs using streams, we achieved 698,000 samples/s (a 4.17× speedup). The problem size stayed fixed, but we added GPUs to go faster. This is strong scaling.

regions.label: text
regions.text: ¡ Strong scaling example —In the pipeline parallelism test, we processed 256 batches of size 64 (a fixed problem). With one GPU, throughput was ~600,000 samples/s. With four GPUs using streams, we achieved 698,000 samples/s (a 4.17× speedup). The problem size stayed fixed, but we added GPUs to go faster. This is strong scaling. ¡ Weak scaling example —The tensor parallelism sweep in table 10.1 shows the weak-scaling effect along the problem-size axis: growing the problem from 4096^3 to 12288^3 multiplies the compute by 27×, but the measured 8-GPU step time by only 8.4× (0.22 ms to 1.85 ms), because the fixed communication cost is amor tized over more arithmetic. Per-GPU shard throughput held at roughly 500–750 TFLOPS across the whole sweep. That is the regime real systems aim for: scale the work per GPU up until compute, not communication, dominates the step.

If yes, that’s perfect weak scaling. If it takes 1.2 ms, that’s 83% weak scaling efficiency. Large training runs care more about weak scaling, because extra GPUs usually go to a larger model rather than a faster run of the same one. The questions that matter day to day are, does the model fit, and does each GPU stay busy? Pipeline parallelism (which we implemented) typically shows good strong scaling up to 8 to 16 GPUs; then efficiency drops as communication dominates. Tensor parallelism shows excellent weak scaling: if you double the model size and double the GPUs, effi ciency stays high. A single node’s GPUs can hold only so much. When a node reaches that limit, com bine the three strategies: data parallelism gives each GPU a different batch, tensor par allelism splits wide layers across the GPUs, and pipeline parallelism splits model depth across stages. Each strategy targets a different dimension: batch size, layer width, or model depth.

regions.text: Data parallelism is the simplest and most common form of distributed training. It keeps a complete copy of the model on every GPU and gives each GPU a different batch of training data. Each GPU computes gradients from its batch independently, and then all GPUs average their gradients before updating the model. Because every GPU starts with the same model and updates with the same averaged gradients, all GPUs stay perfectly synchronized. Figure 10.14 shows this replication pattern.

regions.label: abstract
regions.text: FSDP FSDP is an advanced form of data parallelism that addresses the memory limits of stan dard replication. The reason for using it becomes clear once the model no longer fits comfortably on a single GPU. Standard data parallelism requires the full model to fit on each GPU. For a 7B-parameter model at FP16 (2 bytes per parameter), you need 14 GB just for the weights. But that’s not all. You also need 14 GB for gradients (the same size as the weights), plus the Adam optimizer state kept at FP32: a 28 GB master copy of the weights, 28 GB of momentum, and 28 GB of variance. The standard accounting for mixed-precision training is 16 bytes per parameter (see the ZeRO paper at https: / / arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054 ), which for 7B parameters is 112 GB per GPU. An H100 has 80 GB of memory, so the training state alone already does not fit, and that’s before the activations (the intermediate values during the forward pass) and the batch data, which can add another 10 to 20 GB for large models. Standard data paral lelism fails. FSDP solves this by sharding (splitting) everything across GPUs. With eight GPUs, instead of each GPU storing 112 GB, each GPU stores 112 / 8 = 14 GB. Now the model trains comfortably, with room for activations and batch data. If each GPU only has 1/8 of the model weights, it still has to reconstruct the active layer to run the forward pass. FSDP uses AllGather to temporarily reconstruct the full weights for each layer, computes that layer, then immediately discards the gathered weights to free memory. Let’s walk through a forward pass on GPU 0. It needs to compute the first layer. GPU 0 has shard 0 of the layer weights, GPU 1 has shard 1, and so on. GPU 0 calls AllGather to collect all eight shards and reconstruct the complete layer weights. Now GPU 0 has the full weights in memory temporarily. It computes the layer’s output, then discards the gathered weights. Only the 14 GB shard stays in memory. GPU 0 repeats this process for every layer. The backward pass works the same way: AllGather reconstructs the weights and com putes gradients, then ReduceScatter averages gradients across GPUs and distributes the averaged gradients back to their respective shards. Each GPU updates only its own shard of parameters. The tradeoff is communication. Standard data parallelism does one AllReduce per training step. FSDP does AllGather + ReduceScatter for every layer, which moves about 1.5× the data of standard data parallelism. But this enables training models that other wise wouldn’t fit. On eight H100s, you can train a seven-billion-parameter model with FSDP that would be impossible with standard data parallelism. This is the same basic idea used by PyTorch’s FSDP and DeepSpeed’s ZeRO family of optimizers. When the model no longer fits with standard data parallelism, sharding

The standard accounting for mixed-precision training is 16 bytes per parameter (see the ZeRO paper at https: / / arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054 ), which for 7B parameters is 112 GB per GPU. Standard data paral lelism fails. FSDP solves this by sharding (splitting) everything across GPUs. With eight GPUs, instead of each GPU storing 112 GB, each GPU stores 112 / 8 = 14 GB. This is the same basic idea used by PyTorch’s FSDP and DeepSpeed’s ZeRO family of optimizers. SXM GPUs are modules mounted on a custom GPU baseboard. The entire server is designed around the GPUs, not the other way around. Power is delivered through the motherboard at up to 700 W per GPU (compared to 300 to 450 W for PCIe). Most importantly, all eight GPUs are connected via an NVLink fabric built into the moth erboard, giving each GPU 900 GB/s of total NVLink bandwidth (18 links, reachable toward any peer through NVSwitch).

regions.text: The starting point for most distributed training is data parallelism. When your model fits comfortably on a single GPU but training is too slow, data parallelism offers the eas iest path to speedup. This approach is built into PyTorch’s DistributedDataParallel and TensorFlow’s distribution strategies, making it nearly transparent to users. Data parallelism scales well across a single node’s GPUs before communication overhead becomes significant. The main tradeoff is that batch size must scale with GPU count, which can sometimes hurt convergence if the batch becomes too large.

regions.text: 11.1 Why CUTLASS matters So far, cuBLAS has been the default answer for GEMM-heavy workloads. We hand it our matrices, and it returns fast, reliable results. For a large class of problems, that is exactly the right choice. The reason to look beyond it is that deep learning layers are rarely just a GEMM . They are usually a sequence of operations: a GEMM , a bias add, an activation, and sometimes more. The following listing shows the kind of sequence we would prefer to fuse.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Each of these operations—the matrix multiply, the bias add, and the ReLU— traditionally requires a separate kernel launch. Each launch has overhead, and more importantly, each one involves writing intermediate results back to global GPU mem ory ( D and E in our example) only to immediately read them back in the next kernel. This round trip to DRAM is one of the most expensive things we can do on a GPU. This is where CUTLASS comes in. CUTLASS is not a library in the same sense as cuBLAS. It is a collection of C++ templates that gives us the building blocks to construct our own high-performance kernels. It matters when the library path is close but not quite right: when we need control over tiling, data movement, or the epilogue, not just a faster torch.matmul . Imagine rewriting our PyTorch example into a single CUDA kernel. The output of the matrix multiplication would never leave the high-speed registers or shared mem ory of the streaming multiprocessors (SMs). The bias addition and ReLU application would happen on the fly, right before the final result is written to global memory just once. The performance gains from eliminating those extra memory round trips can be substantial, though the tradeoff still has to be measured against strong framework or cuBLAS baselines. regions.text: To understand how CUTLASS achieves high performance, we need to revisit how matrix multiplication is mapped to the GPU’s execution model. The core principle is hierarchical decomposition . We take a large problem and break it down into smaller pieces that fit neatly into the different levels of the GPU’s hierarchy: grids, threadblocks, warps, and threads. Imagine our goal is to compute C = A x B , where A , B , and C are large matrices. CUTLASS views this not as a single massive operation but as a grid of smaller, independent matrix multiplications. Figure 11.1 shows the hierarchy we will keep referring back to through out the chapter.

Finally, each individual thread within a warp handles a tiny portion of the computation, typically accumulating just a few values in its own registers. This hierarchical approach maximizes data reuse by keeping tiles in fast shared memory for multiple computations before moving on to the next set of data, minimizing the number of slow trips to global DRAM.

regions.label: text
regions.text: This configuration tells CUTLASS that we’re performing a mixed-precision multiply in which the input matrices A and B use a 16-bit floating point, but intermediate accu mulations happen in a 32-bit floating point. With FP16 inputs, a long inner-product sum accumulated in FP16 loses precision as small terms are swamped by the growing sum: once the running total is large enough, each new term is smaller than the sum’s least significant bit and is silently dropped. It can also overflow past FP16’s maximum of 65,504. Promoting the accumulator to FP32 is what keeps the calculation numeri cally stable. The matrices are stored in row-major order, which is standard for C-style arrays. The TileShape directly implements our tile hierarchy, telling CUTLASS that each thread block will compute a 128 × 256 tile of the output matrix C , with the thread block iterating by loading 128 × 64 tiles from A and 64 × 256 tiles from B into shared

regions.text: Composing the kernel with CollectiveBuilder Once we have our definitions, we use CollectiveBuilder to compose the two main parts of our kernel: the Mainloop and the Epilogue . The following listing shows the relevant snippet.

regions.text: using GemmKernel = cutlass::gemm::kernel::GemmUniversal< Shape<int, int, int>, CollectiveMainloop, CollectiveEpilogue >;

regions.label: text
regions.text: CollectiveBuilder automatically selects and the most efficient implementation details for scheduling instructions and moving data based on the high-level configuration we provided. CollectiveMainloop handles the core A × B computation: loading tiles from global to shared memory, managing the computation pipeline, and performing the matrix-multiply-accumulate operations within the thread block. Collective Epilogue takes the accumulated result from the main loop, performs any final operations, and stores it to the output matrix D in global memory. Finally, GemmUniversal stitches these two parts together into a complete, runnable kernel.

regions.label: text
regions.text: One detail in the CollectiveBuilder signature is worth pulling out: the AlignmentA , AlignmentB , AlignmentC , and AlignmentD parameters. These parameters tell CUTLASS, in elements, how the rows (for RowMajor operands) of each matrix are aligned in mem ory, and they are not independent of the TileShape . CUTLASS uses the alignment to pick the widest legal vectorized load/store instructions for moving tiles between global, shared, and register memory, so the alignment values you choose must be compati ble with the K- and N-dimensions of the tile shape (here Shape<_128, _256, _64> ). For 16-bit operands on Hopper, an alignment of eight elements (a 128-bit access) is the common choice, and it divides cleanly into the inner-tile dimensions chosen earlier. If you change the tile shape, you may need to revisit the alignment values to keep the chosen vector width legal.

regions.text: One detail in the CollectiveBuilder signature is worth pulling out: the AlignmentA , AlignmentB , AlignmentC , and AlignmentD parameters. These parameters tell CUTLASS, in elements, how the rows (for RowMajor operands) of each matrix are aligned in mem ory, and they are not independent of the TileShape . CUTLASS uses the alignment to pick the widest legal vectorized load/store instructions for moving tiles between global, shared, and register memory, so the alignment values you choose must be compati ble with the K- and N-dimensions of the tile shape (here Shape<_128, _256, _64> ). For 16-bit operands on Hopper, an alignment of eight elements (a 128-bit access) is the common choice, and it divides cleanly into the inner-tile dimensions chosen earlier. If you change the tile shape, you may need to revisit the alignment values to keep the chosen vector width legal.

regions.text: The host code is responsible for the standard CUDA logistics: allocating memory on the device, copying input data from the host, and eventually copying the result back. The key CUTLASS-specific part is the creation of the Arguments struct. This struct packages up all the information the kernel needs to run: the problem dimensions ( M , N , K ), pointers to the device memory for the matrices, and their strides (how to move from one row or column to the next in memory). With the arguments prepared, we simply initialize() the gemm_op object and then call run() to launch the kernel on the GPU.

regions.text: CuTe allows us to perform “layout algebra.” We can programmatically slice, tile, and partition these layouts to create new views of the data without ever moving the data itself. This is exactly what CUTLASS does internally to manage the complex mapping of tiles from global memory through shared memory and into the registers of each thread. It’s the engine that powers the hierarchical decomposition we saw earlier.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Finding the optimal tile shape is a process of experimentation. The best shape depends on the GPU architecture (e.g., the amount of shared memory per SM), the data types used, and the specific dimensions of the matrices in your workload. The CUTLASS profiler is a practical tool for sweeping through different tile shapes to find the best one empirically. A tile shape tuned for one GPU and one matrix size may not perform as well on another GPU, another shape, or with fewer free SMs, so tune across the shapes and GPUs the kernel will actually run on, not just the case you care about.

regions.text: High-performance kernels almost always use software pipelining to hide the latency of loading data from global memory. This is also known as double-buffering .

regions.text: StageCountAutoCarveout tells CUTLASS to choose the number of pipeline stages based on the amount of shared memory available after reserving space for the epilogue’s needs. More stages can improve the kernel’s ability to hide latency, but each additional stage requires more shared memory. For recent architectures like Hopper, which have hardware support for asynchronous memory transfers (Tensor Memory Accelerator), deeper pipelines are often beneficial.

regions.text: Swapping this FusionOp into the CollectiveEpilogue builder takes one more change. The EpilogueScheduleAuto policy from our baseline kernel supports only the plain linear-combination epilogue; CUTLASS rejects any other fusion operator with a com pile-time error that tells us to pick a TMA warp-specialized schedule. The fix is to name the schedules explicitly: cutlass::epilogue::TmaWarpSpecializedCooperative in the epilogue builder, paired with cutlass::gemm::KernelTmaWarpSpecializedCooperative as the main loop kernel schedule. With that pair in place, the builder generates a ker nel that performs the entire matmul -bias-ReLU sequence in a single launch, keeping intermediate data in the GPU’s fastest memories. This is one of the main reasons to choose CUTLASS over a precompiled library like cuBLAS when a standard library call sequence is no longer a good fit.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Modern deep learning workloads use a “precision ladder” that trades off accuracy for performance. FP32 offers full precision and excellent accuracy but is memory and compute intensive. FP16/BF16 provides half precision and is widely used for training and inference. FP8 uses 8-bit floating point with E4M3/E5M2 formats and is emerging as the standard for inference. FP4 uses just 4 bits per value with 1 sign bit, 2 exponent bits, and 1 mantissa bit, enabling 2× the throughput of FP8 and 4× that of FP16 (each precision halving roughly doubles tensor core throughput, as the B200 rows of table 7.1 shows), though it requires sophisticated scaling techniques to maintain numerical stability.

regions.title: Modern deep learning workloads use a “precision ladder” that trades off accuracy for performance. FP32 offers full precision and excellent accuracy but is memory and compute intensive. FP16/BF16 provides half precision and is widely used for training and inference. FP8 uses 8-bit floating point with E4M3/E5M2 formats and is emerging as the standard for inference. FP4 uses just 4 bits per value with 1 sign bit, 2 exponent bits, and 1 mantissa bit, enabling 2× the throughput of FP8 and 4× that of FP16 (each precision halving roughly doubles tensor core throughput, as the B200 rows of table 7.1 shows), though it requires sophisticated scaling techniques to maintain numerical stability.

regions.text: FP4 is not a universal replacement for higher-precision formats. This level of perfor mance makes it viable for memory-bound workloads where data movement dominates execution time, large models that are challenging to fit in memory, inference optimiza tion where accuracy can be maintained through quantization techniques, and special ized training scenarios where reduced-precision training is acceptable. The Blackwell architecture’s native FP4 support makes these use cases increasingly practical for pro duction deployments.

regions.label: text
regions.text: The profiler’s real power comes from its ability to sweep through many options to help you find the best configuration for your needs. You can give the profiler a problem size and ask it to run all available GEMM kernels to find the fastest one. You can provide a list of thread block tile shapes to test, and the profiler will benchmark each one and report the winner. The profiler automatically runs a CPU-based reference implementa tion to verify that the GPU results are correct within a given tolerance.

regions.label: number
regions.text: 11.6 Profiling and verification To measure a kernel’s performance and check its correctness, CUTLASS ships a com mand-line tool, the CUTLASS Profiler. The profiler is an executable ( cutlass_profiler ) that lives in the tools/profiler directory of the CUTLASS build. It can launch and benchmark any kernel that has been instantiated in the CUTLASS library. Its basic usage is straightforward, as shown in the following listing.

regions.label: number
regions.text: Listing 11.16 Using cutlass_profiler from the command line

regions.label: number
regions.text: ./tools/profiler/cutlass_profiler --kernel=<kernel_name> --m=<M> --n=<N> --k=<K>

regions.label: number
regions.text: This command runs the specified kernel for the given problem size ( M , N , K ) and reports its performance, typically in TFLOP/s. The profiler’s real power comes from its ability to sweep through many options to help you find the best configuration for your needs. You can give the profiler a problem size and ask it to run all available GEMM kernels to find the fastest one. You can provide a list of thread block tile shapes to test, and the profiler will benchmark each one and report the winner. The profiler automatically runs a CPU-based reference implementa tion to verify that the GPU results are correct within a given tolerance. Our unofficial/single_gpu_gemm.cu example contains its own simple benchmark ing and verification logic within its main() function, which is great for a self-contained example. The following listing shows that helper.

regions.label: number
regions.text: Listing 11.17 Benchmark and verification helper inside the sample GEMM

regions.label: number
regions.text: auto start = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now(); for (int i = 0; i < bench_iters; i++) { gemm_op.run(); } CUDA_CHECK(cudaDeviceSynchronize()); auto end = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();

regions.label: number
regions.text: double time_ms = std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>(end - start). count() / bench_iters; double tflops = (2.0 * M * N * K) / (time_ms * 1e9);

regions.label: number
regions.text: std::cout << "Average time: " << time_ms << " ms" << std::endl; std::cout << "Performance: " << tflops << " TFLOPS" << std::endl;

regions.label: text
regions.text: 11.7 Beyond a single GPU: Distributed GEMM So far, we have focused on maximizing the performance of a GEMM on a single GPU. Chapter 10 covered the communication side of multi-GPU execution with NCCL and parallelism strategies; now we connect those ideas back to CUTLASS. CUTLASS pro vides the building blocks for this world as well, enabling the construction of distributed GEMMs that can use the combined power of multiple GPUs within a node. The core idea behind a distributed GEMM is to shard the matrices across GPUs and have each GPU compute a portion of the result. This approach requires careful coordi nation and communication, typically using a library like NVIDIA’s NCCL to exchange data between GPUs over high-speed interconnects like NVLink. One point of terminology first: the ClusterShape we saw earlier has nothing to do with multiple GPUs. It configures the thread block cluster, a group of thread blocks co-scheduled on neighboring SMs of a single GPU so they can share distributed shared memory and multicast TMA loads. regions.text: 11.7 Beyond a single GPU: Distributed GEMM So far, we have focused on maximizing the performance of a GEMM on a single GPU. Chapter 10 covered the communication side of multi-GPU execution with NCCL and parallelism strategies; now we connect those ideas back to CUTLASS. CUTLASS pro vides the building blocks for this world as well, enabling the construction of distributed GEMMs that can use the combined power of multiple GPUs within a node. The core idea behind a distributed GEMM is to shard the matrices across GPUs and have each GPU compute a portion of the result. This approach requires careful coordi nation and communication, typically using a library like NVIDIA’s NCCL to exchange data between GPUs over high-speed interconnects like NVLink. One point of terminology first: the ClusterShape we saw earlier has nothing to do with multiple GPUs. It configures the thread block cluster, a group of thread blocks co-scheduled on neighboring SMs of a single GPU so they can share distributed shared memory and multicast TMA loads. Multi-GPU GEMM is a separate, experimental CUTLASS feature: Distributed GEMM ( examples/65_distributed_gemm for Hopper, examples/82_blackwell_distributed_gemm for Blackwell), which parameterizes a ker nel by its tensor-parallel rank and overlaps communication with computation. The book.cu/9_cutlass/unofficial/multi_gpu_gemm.cu and book.cu/9_cutlass/official/ official_multi_gpu_gemm/ examples provide a simpler starting point, showing how to initialize NCCL communicators and launch a kernel on multiple devices. There are many strategies for distributing a GEMM, such as splitting the M dimen sion, the N dimension, or both, each with different communication patterns and performance characteristics. CUTLASS provides the flexibility to implement these strategies, such as AllGather + GEMM, where each GPU has a shard of the input matrix A , and an AllGather collective is used to collect the full matrix on every GPU before a local GEMM is performed, or GEMM + ReduceScatter, where each GPU computes a partial result and a ReduceScatter collective is used to sum the partial results and dis tribute the final output shards. Building efficient distributed kernels is a complex topic that goes beyond the scope of this chapter, but it’s important to know that the same principles of tiled decomposi tion and layout-centric design that we’ve learned apply here as well, extended across the new dimension of multiple devices.

It separates a tensor’s logical shape from its physical strides and supports compile-time layout algebra such as slicing, tiling, and partitioning. ¡ TileShape is the most important tuning knob and trades arithmetic intensity against shared-memory and register pressure. regions.text: ¡ CUTLASS is a C++ template library, not a binary like cuBLAS. It provides build ing blocks for GEMM kernels with custom tiling, fused epilogues, and explicit control over data movement. ¡ CUTLASS decomposes a GEMM hierarchically, partitioning it into tiles pro cessed at the thread block, warp, and thread levels, keeping data resident in shared memory and registers rather than round-tripping through DRAM. ¡ CollectiveBuilder (CUTLASS 3.x) composes a kernel from a Mainloop and an Epilogue ; the host launches it through GemmUniversalAdapter and an Arguments struct that packages problem dimensions, device pointers, and strides. ¡ CuTe is the layout system underlying modern CUTLASS. It separates a tensor’s logical shape from its physical strides and supports compile-time layout algebra such as slicing, tiling, and partitioning. ¡ TileShape is the most important tuning knob and trades arithmetic intensity against shared-memory and register pressure. Pipeline staging (e.g., StageCount AutoCarveout ) hides global-memory latency by prefetching the next tile while the current tile is being computed. ¡ Epilogue fusion (e.g., LinCombPerRowBiasEltAct ) folds bias additions and activa tions into the GEMM kernel, eliminating the extra launches and DRAM round trips that a naive matmul → bias → ReLU sequence would incur. ¡ CUTLASS 2.x targets Ampere with explicit ThreadblockShape , WarpShape , and InstructionShape declarations. CUTLASS 3.x targets Hopper and newer with declarative tile and cluster shapes that let CollectiveBuilder pick schedules spe cific to the architecture. ¡ Blackwell FP4 kernels use block-scaled layouts with per-block 8-bit scale factors (UE8M0 for MXFP4, UE4M3 for NVFP4) to maintain numerical stability while running at FP4 throughput on TCGen05 tensor cores. ¡ cutlass_profiler benchmarks any instantiated kernel and sweeps tile-shape configurations against a CPU reference for correctness; self-contained har nesses inside the sample GEMMs measure TFLOPS over many iterations using chrono::high_resolution_clock . ¡ ClusterShape configures the on-GPU thread block cluster, not multi-GPU exe cution. Multi-GPU GEMMs come from CUTLASS’s experimental distributed GEMM examples or from sharding by hand, exchanging shards via NCCL collec tives such as AllGather + GEMM or GEMM + ReduceScatter over NVLink.

regions.text: Chapter 10 stayed within one multi-GPU server. Scaling that work across servers requires infrastructure that sits outside CUDA itself. If you are operating a GPU cluster with hun dreds or thousands of GPUs, you need cluster orchestration tools, such as SLURM for job scheduling, Kubernetes with Kubeflow for containerized machine learning work loads, or Ray for distributed computing with autoscaling and fault tolerance. These tools manage resource allocation, queues, and job coordination across shared clusters.

A poor match between topology and workload can turn the interconnect into the bottleneck and erase much of the benefit of scaling out.

regions.text: 12.1.2 Convolution-heavy architectures

regions.label: footer
regions.text: We focused heavily on transformers, MLPs, and matrix multiplication. That matches a lot of modern language model work, but it is not the whole field of deep learning. Convolutional neural networks still matter for image classification, detection, seg mentation, robotics, medical imaging, and many edge workloads. Diffusion models and multimodal models often mix attention with convolution-like image operations, resampling, normalization, and layout conversions. Those architectures rely on different kernels, such as conv2d , maxpool2d , batchnorm2d , resize operators, and image/tensor layout transforms, but the intuition you built in this book transfers directly. You implemented conv2d and maxpool2d in chapter 3 as practice kernels. BatchNorm is similar to LayerNorm, but it reduces and normalizes across dif ferent dimensions. Modern architectures mostly reorganize these kernel families with different shapes, schedules, and data flows. If you understand GEMM optimization, as you do after chapter 6, you can also under stand modern convolution implementations. Frameworks often lower convolutions into matrix-multiplication-like problems using techniques such as im2col , implicit GEMM, or Winograd transforms. The reduction concept you learned in softmax applies to maxpool but across a 2D window instead of a 1D sequence. The CUDA skill is recogniz ing the same memory and parallelism problems when the tensor shapes change.

regions.label: footer
regions.text: 12.1.3 The Blackwell TCGen05 instructions

regions.label: footer
regions.text: In chapter 7, we covered tensor cores across multiple generations: MMA and WMMA, introduced with Volta (and extended with new precisions on Turing and Ampere), and then WGMMA for Hopper. But we stopped before Blackwell’s TCGen05 instructions, the next-generation tensor core programming model that supports FP4 and replaces WGMMA with improved efficiency. I chose to omit these topics because raw TCGen05 programming adds complexity without teaching new concepts. The programming patterns you learned with MMA and WGMMA transfer directly to TCGen05. The core concepts, including fragment lay outs, tile hierarchies, and asynchronous operations, remain the same. Only the specific instructions change. For readers who want to target Blackwell (B200 GPUs are available on AWS, GCP, and Azure), CUTLASS 4.x provides the cleanest path.

regions.text: 12.1.2 Convolution-heavy architectures

regions.label: footer
regions.text: We focused heavily on transformers, MLPs, and matrix multiplication. That matches a lot of modern language model work, but it is not the whole field of deep learning. Convolutional neural networks still matter for image classification, detection, seg mentation, robotics, medical imaging, and many edge workloads. Diffusion models and multimodal models often mix attention with convolution-like image operations, resampling, normalization, and layout conversions. Those architectures rely on different kernels, such as conv2d , maxpool2d , batchnorm2d , resize operators, and image/tensor layout transforms, but the intuition you built in this book transfers directly. You implemented conv2d and maxpool2d in chapter 3 as practice kernels. BatchNorm is similar to LayerNorm, but it reduces and normalizes across dif ferent dimensions. Modern architectures mostly reorganize these kernel families with different shapes, schedules, and data flows. If you understand GEMM optimization, as you do after chapter 6, you can also under stand modern convolution implementations. Frameworks often lower convolutions into matrix-multiplication-like problems using techniques such as im2col , implicit GEMM, or Winograd transforms. The reduction concept you learned in softmax applies to maxpool but across a 2D window instead of a 1D sequence. The CUDA skill is recogniz ing the same memory and parallelism problems when the tensor shapes change.

regions.text: 12.1.3 The Blackwell TCGen05 instructions

regions.label: footer
regions.text: In chapter 7, we covered tensor cores across multiple generations: MMA and WMMA, introduced with Volta (and extended with new precisions on Turing and Ampere), and then WGMMA for Hopper. But we stopped before Blackwell’s TCGen05 instructions, the next-generation tensor core programming model that supports FP4 and replaces WGMMA with improved efficiency. I chose to omit these topics because raw TCGen05 programming adds complexity without teaching new concepts. The programming patterns you learned with MMA and WGMMA transfer directly to TCGen05. The core concepts, including fragment lay outs, tile hierarchies, and asynchronous operations, remain the same. Only the specific instructions change. For readers who want to target Blackwell (B200 GPUs are available on AWS, GCP, and Azure), CUTLASS 4.x provides the cleanest path.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Triton: Python-level GPU programming Triton ( https: / /github.com/triton-lang/triton ) is a Python-based domain-specific lan guage (DSL) for writing GPU kernels. It raises the abstraction level so you can work at the tile or block level instead of spelling out every low-level CUDA detail yourself. You write kernels in Python at the block level (think: one block of threads), not at the thread level. The question is, “Where is the bottleneck, and which layer gives me enough con trol to move it?” Stay high-level when the profiler shows that most time is spent in well-optimized library calls, when development speed matters more than squeezing out the last few percent, or when the workload changes too often for a custom kernel to stay useful. Drop lower when the profiler points to a specific operator, memory lay out, synchronization pattern, or fusion opportunity that the higher-level stack cannot express.

regions.text: 12.2.1 Triton: Python-level GPU programming Triton ( https: / /github.com/triton-lang/triton ) is a Python-based domain-specific lan guage (DSL) for writing GPU kernels. It raises the abstraction level so you can work at the tile or block level instead of spelling out every low-level CUDA detail yourself. You write kernels in Python at the block level (think: one block of threads), not at the thread level. Triton handles much of the scheduling and memory-management boiler plate for you, which lets you focus more on the algorithm and less on the mechanics of CUDA. Triton is also hardware agnostic. Your Triton code officially targets NVIDIA GPUs (compute capability 8.0+) and AMD GPUs (ROCm 6.2+), with a CPU backend under development and third-party out-of-tree backends extending it to other accelerators such as neural processing units (NPUs). The promise is, “Write once, run anywhere,” though the real portability story still depends on backend maturity. With compiler-initiated opti mizations and developer- initiated fusion, Triton kernels can approach the performance of tuned CUDA kernels without forcing you to manage the memory hierarchy directly. The integration with PyTorch is particularly compelling. With torch.compile and TorchInductor, PyTorch can automatically generate optimized kernels for your oper ations, often using Triton on GPU backends. You often do not have to write the Triton code yourself. This is still a CUDA book, not a Triton book. Triton matters because it is a major tool in the ecosystem, and learning raw CUDA first makes you better at using Triton. You understand what the compiler is doing under the hood, when it helps, and when you may need to intervene. The practical test is simple: start from a PyTorch or NumPy-like reference; write the Triton version if the framework output is not good enough; then compare cor rectness and latency across the shapes you actually care about. regions.label: text
regions.text: This is where isolated CUDA thinking can mislead you. A single kernel might be faster in a microbenchmark, but the production system might still be bottlenecked on batching policy, memory fragmentation, model loading, network overhead, or the shape distribution of real requests. The right measurement is the end-to-end system: time to first token, intertoken latency, throughput at a target latency, GPU utilization, memory footprint, and reliability under real traffic.

regions.text: 12.3.2 SGLang SGLang ( https: / /github.com/sgl-project/sglang ) focuses on structured generation and efficient constrained decoding. If your application needs JSON outputs, function calling, or grammar-constrained generation, SGLang handles this efficiently. SGLang’s RadixAttention automatically reuses KV cache across requests with similar prefixes. It includes an xGrammar backend for fast structured outputs, cache-aware load balancing, and a batch scheduler designed to keep GPU utilization high. The following listing shows the structured-generation style it targets.

regions.label: text
regions.text: ONNX is a serialization format for computation graphs. You train in PyTorch (or JAX or TensorFlow), export the graph to .onnx, and then run it through a run time such as ONNX Runtime, TensorRT, or a hardware-vendor backend. Because the format is shared, the same exported model can run on NVIDIA GPUs through TensorRT, on CPUs through ONNX Runtime, on mobile accelerators, and on edge silicon that does not speak PyTorch natively. The following listing shows the typical export step.

regions.text: The functional style matters because it gives the compiler a cleaner view of the com putation. If a function has no hidden mutation, JAX can trace it, transform it, differen tiate it, batch it, and compile it through XLA. From a CUDA perspective, this means the programmer often describes array programs while the compiler decides how to fuse operations, allocate intermediates, and lower the graph to GPU code.
