regions.label: text
regions.text: We covered kernel-level optimization extensively, but high-level tricks also matter for inference. Speculative decoding generates multiple tokens in parallel by having a small “draft” model propose tokens and a large “verifier” model accept or reject them. Con tinuous batching processes requests as they arrive rather than waiting for full batches. vLLM and SGLang both build this kind of scheduling into their serving models.

regions.text: 12.8 High-level inference tricks We covered kernel-level optimization extensively, but high-level tricks also matter for inference. Speculative decoding generates multiple tokens in parallel by having a small “draft” model propose tokens and a large “verifier” model accept or reject them. Con tinuous batching processes requests as they arrive rather than waiting for full batches. vLLM and SGLang both build this kind of scheduling into their serving models. Prefix caching stores the KV cache for common prefixes, such as system prompts, so every request with the same prefix reuses the same cached KV values. We covered weight quantization in chapter 9, but you can also quantize the KV cache, which saves memory and enables longer contexts, and activations, which saves bandwidth during inference. Model compilation tools like TensorRT and torch.compile can fuse opera tions, remove unnecessary copies, and generate specialized code for your model archi tecture and hardware. These techniques can produce substantial additional speedups on top of optimized kernels, though the gains are highly workload-dependent. The vLLM documentation ( https: / /docs.vllm.ai ) is the most practical resource for this serving-level optimization, and Simon Boehm’s blog ( https: / /siboehm.com ) is the classic walk-through of the under lying kernel-level work, taking a CUDA GEMM step by step to near-cuBLAS performance.

regions.label: text
regions.text: NVIDIA publishes official bandwidth figures only for global memory; the on-chip tiers are best reasoned about from the hardware itself. Shared memory delivers up to 128 bytes per clock per SM (32 banks, 4 bytes each), which, across all SMs at boost clock, works out to roughly 18 TB/s aggregate on the RTX 3090 and roughly 33 TB/s on the H100: an order of magnitude above global memory, which is exactly why tiling into shared memory pays off. Registers are faster still, feeding operands effectively every cycle.

regions.label: text

regions.text: D.3.4 PyTorch C++ extension boilerplate If you’re binding CUDA kernels to PyTorch, here’s the standard pattern:

regions.label: number
regions.text: // my_cuda_ops.cu #include <torch/extension.h> #include <cuda_runtime.h>

regions.label: number
regions.text: // CUDA kernel (in .cu file or separate header) template <typename T> __global__ void my_kernel(T* output, const T* input, int n) { int idx = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x; if (idx < n) { output[idx] = input[idx] * 2.0f; // Example operation } }

regions.label: number
regions.text: // C++ wrapper function torch::Tensor my_cuda_forward(torch::Tensor input) { // Input validation TORCH_CHECK(input.is_cuda(), "input must be a CUDA tensor"); TORCH_CHECK(input.is_contiguous(), "input must be contiguous");

regions.label: number
regions.text: // Allocate output auto output = torch::empty_like(input);

regions.label: number
regions.text: // Launch configuration int n = input.numel(); int threads = 256; int blocks = (n + threads - 1) / threads;

regions.label: number
regions.text: // Dispatch based on dtype AT_DISPATCH_FLOATING_TYPES(input.scalar_type(), "my_kernel", ([&] { my_kernel<scalar_t><<<blocks, threads>>>( output.data_ptr<scalar_t>(), input.data_ptr<scalar_t>(), n ); }));

regions.label: number
regions.text: // Check for errors cudaError_t err = cudaGetLastError(); TORCH_CHECK(err == cudaSuccess, "CUDA kernel failed: ", cudaGetErrorString(err));

regions.label: number
regions.text: return output; }

regions.label: number
regions.text: // PyBind11 bindings PYBIND11_MODULE(TORCH_EXTENSION_NAME, m) { m.def("forward", &my_cuda_forward, "My CUDA operation (CUDA)"); }

regions.text: D.3.5 Template best practices Do: ¡ Use templates for type genericity ( float , half , int , etc.). ¡ Use compile-time constants for tile sizes (enables optimizations). ¡ Use constexpr for compile-time calculations. ¡ Add static_assert to catch configuration errors early. ¡ Document template parameters clearly. Don’t: ¡ Over-templatize simple kernels (adds compilation time). ¡ Use templates for runtime-variable parameters (use function arguments). ¡ Instantiate too many template combinations (binary bloat). ¡ Mix template metaprogramming with complex device code (which can be hard to debug).

regions.text: As shown in chapter 6, profiling metrics can be misleading: ¡ High memory throughput ≠ good —Naive kernels often show high utilization from wasteful, uncoalesced access. ¡ Low occupancy ≠ bad —GEMM with 16% occupancy can outperform 66% occu pancy if arithmetic intensity is high. ¡ Cache hit rate context —High L1 hits in naive GEMM (95%) mean the working set fits in cache; low hits in tiled GEMM (12%) mean we’re accessing more unique data (better!) Profiling workflow: 1 Baseline —Profile a naive implementation to identify the bottleneck type. 2 Optimize —Make a targeted change (coalescing, tiling, etc.). 3 Measure —Re-profile to verify improvement in relevant metrics. 4 Iterate —Focus on the new bottleneck revealed by profiling. 5 Validate —Compare final kernel duration against baseline and libraries (cuBLAS, cuDNN).
